speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to raise a question of privilege relating to the proceedings yesterday, and to say to Your Honour that if you will turn to page 22 of yesterday's Hansard, near the bottom of the second column, you will find there these words-and it is with respect to these words that I want to raise the question of privilege now:
Mr. Graydon: When you consider the point of order raised by the hon. member for Temis-couata, Mr. Speaker, will you please advise the house how you are able, under any of the rules of the house, to bring in at page 2 of the order paper a motion which appears at page 12, without the unanimous consent of the house?
I must say I was greatly concerned over that procedure. Then Your Honour said, according to Hansard:
Notices of motions standing on the order paper under the head "government notices of motions" can be moved under the head "motions" in routine proceedings on the order paper. I would ask the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and the hon. member for Temiscouata, to turn to page 219 of Bourinot where it states:
Routine motions includes only motions relating to the business of the house.
Then you go on to say you feel that would be a sufficient answer.
My question of privilege is this. I listened to you, very carefully and intently, yesterday as you read the words:
Notices of motions standing on the order paper under the head "government notices of motions" can be moved under the head "motions" in routine proceedings on the order paper.
Those words, as we understood here, certainly as I understood them, listening very intently, were read directly from Bourinot, and when I heard the authoritative words of Bourinot, as I sat in my seat, I felt, as I usually do in the shadow of the great Bourinot, somewhat eclipsed, with the result that I then sat down and discontinued my argument. It is no reflection upon Your Honour, Mr. Speaker, if I say that I do not feel quite so
much eclipsed now, because these words apparently do not appear in Bourinot. All that appears in Bourinot is:
Routine motions includes only motions relating to the business of the house.
Obviously, unless there is something in Bourinot which actually gives this precedent, then we are entitled to some explanation of the position of both the government and Your Honour with relation to the changing of the whole program of the house, as was done yesterday, and the moving of proceedings from page 12 to page 2 without the unanimous consent of the house.
I want to raise that point because I think all members will want a clarification of it, since it goes to the very roots of our rights as members.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, December 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. A. Dion for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Air. Speaker, my first word on behalf of the party associated with me is one of congratulation both to the mover and to the seconder of the address in reply. May I congratulate the mover upon his most excellent speech delivered in French, and the seconder upon his well phrased observations.
We would also associate ourselves with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Bracken) in extending to the Prime Minister (Mr. Alackenzie King) our congratulations upon his receiving the distinction of being invested with the OrHer of Merit. I believe that this was not only a recognition of the long service the Prime Minister has rendered our country, but also a recognition by His Majesty of the contribution made by Canada to the allied cause during the second great war. I congratulate him most sincerely.
I should like first to deal with the question directed to me yesterday by the hon. member for Peel (Air. Graydon). He made a statement which, upon thinking it over, I believe he will consider as having been somewhat beneath his dignity. He made an accusation against this party which, in view of the record,
I believe could have been levelled with more consistency and with more authority against the party with which he is associated-because at least we have been consistent in resisting

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
the removal of controls and subsidies. These are the matters under discussion today. I have no hesitation, however, in answering the hon. member's questions, and I will deal first with the one regarding farm prices.
Ever since the C.C.F. came into existence we have fought for orderly marketing with producer control and parity prices. Unlike my hon. friends we did not criticize the wheat agreement because in the words of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) on August 15, 1946, as reported on page 4822 of Hansard:
This, Mr. Chairman, is the end of the government's policy of selling cheap wheat to the hungry nations of the world other than Britain, and it will be a handicap to us in trying to build up a market in all these other countries which so interpret this arrangement.
On the other hand on the same day I said this:
In the event of costs of production rising, as they will do largely because of the government's failure to maintain the price ceilings, any difference there may be between what the farmer receives for his wheat and the increased cost of production should be made up out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
I repeat that parity prices negotiated by the producers with representatives of the government are the keynote of our policy; not prices set by speculators or prices set arbitrarily by the government.
I believe the leader of the opposition was present when committee No. 2 of the united nations was sitting last year and when the late Mayor LaGuardia of New York, appearing before that committee as secretary-general of UNRRA, made the statement that the farmers will never get a square deal, nor will the consumers of the world get their food at proper prices, until every gambling grain exchange, whether it be in Chicago, Liverpool or Winnipeg, has been closed forever. Last evening we listened to the leader of the opposition state that he was in favour of open-market trading, as well as in favour of the wheat board-two conflicting statements, may I say.
Then, when the hon. member for Peel asked me his second question he resorted to a trick. He and his friends have demanded that parliament shall not invade provincial rights. Parliament has handed back to the provinces control of labour conditions, including wages. We have retained jurisdiction over prices, and hence the C.C.F. has devoted its attention to that phase of our economy over which the house has control. In other words we are minding our own business strictly within our rights, as the Tory party is insisting the house should do. When we have the national labour code which we desire it will be proper for the house to discuss the best means of obtaining 5849-6J
decent wages and living standards for those who work in industry. Meantime rising prices over which we in parliament have control are bearing heavily upon hundreds of thousands of people existing on substandard incomes in this country. Let me say that the C.C.F. will never agree to the freezing of wages at substandard levels, which is what my hon. friends mean when they talk of immediate wage controls.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Do not smear everybody when you are talking. That is not right, and you know it is not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I did not want to leave the matter there without making a positive statement on behalf of this party. When this parliament has jurisdiction the C.C.F. would establish minimum standards of wages and of living, adequate to maintain a decent Canadian standard of life. Next, we would establish proper relationships between wages, prices and profits in a balanced and planned economy. That, of course, involves democratic controls, this to be achieved through properly constituted boards representative both of government and of labour. Next, the objective in mind would be to increase production and consumption, thus progressively raising the standard of living of all our people.
Having stated the C.C.F. position, may I ask my hon. friends, particularly the hon. member for Peel, a question? This is our policy, but will the Tory party declare its policy in equally unequivocal terms? I listened yesterday with great care hoping to hear an outline of the Tory policy, but there was none. There was a great deal of talk about Jeremiah, and of the fact that perhaps the Canadian people were not getting the goods they required because there was too much money in supply for the goods that were available. The hon. member went on to say something about keeping more in this country. The world is starving, and I remember also something that Jeremiah said in Lamentations:
They that be slain with the sword are better than they that be slain with hunger: for these pine away, stricken through for want of the fruits of the field.
My hon. friend should remember that when they talk about keeping more goods in this country and in that manner trying to keep down prices.
I want to turn to the address for a moment.

He seldom speaks, but when, he does speak he does not say anything that is worth listening to.
Shorn of all talk of general and unprecedented levels of employment and of national income, of which the speech from the throne reminds us, the fact is that this country now faces an economic crisis of the first magnitude. I take it that that is why parliament is in session now. We are called upon to recognize the fact that the war did not end in August, 1945; neither did wartime conditions end at that time. But just as in 1919, in 1945 the cry went up from big business for a return of what they called "normalcy". The same cry went up; the same interests demanded freedom from all controls and the immediate return to what they were pleased to call free enterprise.
When parliament met after the last general election all the parties except the one which I have the honour to lead were committed to the removal of wartime controls. True, the Liberal party had qualified its promise to remove controls with the phrase "as rapidly as circumstances would permit," but so great was the pressure from the vested interests that "the circumstances" was interpreted to mean the removal of large groups of controls within a few months of the election. -

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Do you consider the farmers as being vested interests?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The farmers did not ask for the removal of controls. Every one of the farm organizations wanted the grain exchange closed and the continuance of trading through government boards. The C.C.E. alone warned that just as shortages after the first war created high prices and grave economic and social difficulties, so in the post-war period with the need of the world greater there would be similar shortages. The government believed that in 1944. I have in my hand an advertisement published by the authority of the government of Canada on November 23, 1914. It reads:
The Road Back Without Price Control
The worst inflation came after the war the last time ... to be followed by disastrous deflation, unemployment and confusion. For Canada to manage successfully the change back to peace, maintain employment, and meet the world's competition . . . we must continue to have stable economic conditions. To protect the individual from rising costs of living and later unemployment we must continue to prevent inflation.
To prevent a repetition of the conditions following the last war price control must be maintained as long as inflation threatens us.

As soon as the election was over we found controls being thrown into the discard, with the result that we have the conditions we have today. The annual reports of our chartered banks now appearing in the newspapers warn us that the present economic trends are heading us in the direction of disaster. It is not often that I find myself in agreement with the presidents of our chartered banks, but I do agree with the warnings that they are now giving to the Canadian people in their annual speeches and reports.
Eighteen months ago we should have taken heed of what happened in the United States when congress refused to sanction the continuance of controls. More particularly we should haven taken heed of the sharp increases that followed the removal of controls, except rent controls, in the United States a year ago last September. Indeed we should have been warned by what happened in our own country. Because of the early removal of some basic controls, not only did the prices of decontrolled commodities rise, but followed as they were by permitted increases of So per ton for steel ingots and 12^ per cent increase on farm machinery, costs of production and cost of living rose and this accounted for a growing demand for wage increases and better farm returns in the months that followed. But neither wages nor average farm income ever catch up to rising prices and corporation profits in an inflationary period in a capitalistic economy. Of this I shall have more to say in a few moments.
Suffice it to say that in addition to the purchasing groups I have mentioned, pensioners, whether they be veterans of the first or of the second great war, whether they be persons with old age pensions, fixed incomes, or low wages, suffered reductions in an already painfully low standard of living. At a price of 17 cents per quart for milk, the present price in Ottawa, to provide the three quarts per day which government nutritional experts tell us are needed for a couple with three children, would cost 51 cents a day, or $3.57 a week.
In order to provide that a family with an adequate supply of butter, again at today's price in this city of 68 cents per pound, and an adequate supply of bread at 15 cents a loaf; in order to pay for rent and provide fuel, it would take practically all the income of a low income family. In 1942, which is unfortunately the latest year for which we have official figures, according to the government's own bureau of statistics it is estimated that there were 756,300 income recipients in Canada with incomes of less than $500 a year.

The Address-Mr. Caldwell
Of this number, 127,400 were married men. These figures do not include those engaged in agriculture, and in some parts of Canada incomes on the farms are lamentably low. Of course since 1942, a fairly prosperous war year, our total income has risen about one billion dollars this year, or by some ten per cent, but the maldistribution of wealth is still just as great as it was then.
Last week the figures indicating the increase in the cost of living up to the end of October were released by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. They indicated a rise of over 43 per cent since the war began and over 20 per cent since the war ended. That was before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) announced the prohibition of imports from the United States three weeks ago last night. None of us will deny that the prohibition of luxury imports and luxury travel in the United States in view of our dollar shortage was long overdue. But to prohibit the importation of health foods and of necessities, or to place them on a low import quota, if not ill advised, was entirely wrong when the prohibitions were not accompanied by some measures of price control. Of course prices jumped immediately; for under so-called private enterprise scarcity gives the golden opportunity for high profits. That is what powerful monopolies and cartels have always plotted to achieve. That is why, when basic commodities were about to become in short supply recently, prices rose at once. How they jumped our daily newspapers recorded. Onions, cabbage, carrots, parsnips, spinach and celery rose from 50 to 75 per cent in price on the Toronto market, so the Canadian Importers and Traders Association reported. Potatoes in the hands of jobbers and retailers rose from two to three dollars a bag-and may I add that the producer got none of these price increases. In Montreal the increases were even higher. The Montreal Gazette reported that a Toronto survey showed that the price of general canned goods stood on the average 100 per cent higher than a year ago. Who got these increases? The Toronto Star reported on November 25 that official surveys had been made of how the price increases on various canned vegetables and fresh fruits and fresh vegetables were made up. Generally speaking, so they said, the producers got actually less in 1947 than in 1946. In one case the producer's share was 60 much reduced and the retailer's so much increased that the retailer got almost as much for selling the article as the producer got for growing and harvesting it. As another sample of profiteering by jobbers, the price of British Columbia apples jumped one dollar a box.
The producer did not receive a penny of the increase. Generally speaking, as I said before, the grower did not benefit by these sudden and spectacular price increases.
What did the government do? The Minister of Finance announced the re-establishment of price ceilings on canned tomatoes, corn, peas and peaches. Corn syrup had not yet been decontrolled. These are five, and only five, out of a total of forty-six food items in the bureau of statistics food index, making all together 3-29 of the food index, which makes up only 37 per cent of the present general index cost of living. In other words, the re-establishment of price control on these few items, including corn syrup, which had not been decontrolled, affects about only 1*2 per cent of the prices in the cost of living index.
The government's policy of premature ending of the major activities of the wartime prices and trade board has made the immediate reimposition of price ceilings almost impossible. Only five of the 128 regional offices of the board now remain open. So much for the effect of the government's decontrol policy on fruits and vegetables where the effect was felt immediately by consumers.
Still more disastrous was the removal of price ceilings and subsidies from coarse grains. H. H. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, on November 2 of this year, ten days or so after the ceilings and subsidies had been removed, said:
Nothing that has happened in many years has stirred farmers and dairy farmers throughout Canada to such a high pitch of resentment as has the recent action of the dominion government in removing ceilings and subsidies from coarse grains at this particular time.
The government's action has cut the feet from under the best live stock program we ever had in Canada-a program that not only achieved the greatest production of live stock, dairy and poultry products in our history, but what is more important, established some degree of stability in the whole agricultural program and offered hope for some permanency to this stability in the future.
In any event why were the ceilings removed toward the end of October, when except for grain delivered to the pools, and not yet marketed, barley and oats delivered by hundreds of farmers had passed into the hands of private interests who proceeded to make a killing on the open speculative market?
How does the government propose to compensate the farmers who marketed their grain early, at the request of the government agency, may I say; for they are clearly entitled to recognition and to adequate compensation? Farmers, both those who sold
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

grain and those who bought it, were entitled to believe that the subsidies and ceilings would be maintained for the current crop year. Coming on the heels of the partial failure of feed grain crops in no fewer than five provinces, with resultant shortages, the government's action is all the more reprehensible.
On the other hand the prices of the farmer's bacon, eggs, and livestock, governed by prices under the British contracts, left them at the mercy of grain exchange speculators in the pursuance of their purchases of essential feeding materials. Prices of feed grain jumped- thirty to forty per cent in a week, and the farmers reacted immediately. I was in the west at the time, and I heard hog raisers declare that they were going to kill young pigs as they were farrowed, and ship the sows as soon as they could to the abattoirs. Weaned pigs, which heretofore were worth five dollars or more, were offered for sale by western farmers in certain parts for fifty cents, with no buyers. In Ontario, farmers were going out of hogs and dairy cattle because they could not afford to buy feed; for, as Mr. Hannam said:
The government's action cut the feet from under the best livestock program we ever had in Canada.
Not that we believe it could not have been a lot better than it was.
The city man does not yet realize what this will mean to him in the near future. Now that ceilings have been removed from feed grains the demand that barriers against the unrestricted sale of live stock and dairy products shall be removed is an understandable result. And the granting of that demand would mean that the Canadian consumer and our hard-pressed overseas customers would become still more the victims of government policy and United States inflation.
Decontrol-decontrol, I repeat-is leading us to inevitable disaster. United States prices without United States levels of income and wages will work hardship and cause endless unrest. As prices rise steeply the organized worker will demand and take legitimate and understandable steps to get more wages. But the packing and processing monopolies will not suffer. Here is a golden opportunity to fill their depleted storage facilities with cheap meat, perchance for export to the United States, or for sale at higher prices to the Canadian consumer, who will be denied protective foods because of high prices. Young and old in Canada will inevitably suffer, and I say that the government must take the full responsibility for its failure to protect the

people's health and interest. But condemnation must be shared by all those who urged these policies upon the country, and not the least of the burden must be shared by the Progressive Conservative party, who now cry aloud about high food prices and at the same time urge policies which would further inflate the general price level for farmers and workers alike.
I have before me the record of some of their statements. In fact I have a number of records, but I will take two or three. In May of this year the party's chief financial critic, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), said, as reported at page 2799 of Hansard:
At the moment it is particularly unfortunate that we here-
That is, I presume, in the Progressive Conservative party.
-who believe in removing controls, and I am one of those, at the present time are at a most unsatisfactory moment, as you might say, from the point of view^ of the people of the class of which I am speaking.
Equally clear was the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), himself a farmer and a Progressive Conservative member of this house, who said, as reported at page 1698 of Hansard of March 24, 1947:
As of November 30, 1946, these freight assistance and feed grain subsidy payments amounted to $105,081,627.62. That is quite an item which the taxpayers of the country had to account for in connection with that system of controls, which to me is not a sound economy for this country.

May I say that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) made the statement that for every $200 million we have spent each year in subsidies and controls, the people of Canada had been saved $2,500,000,000 annually. In other words, for every dollar we spent in controls and subsidies, the Canadian consumer, or the government, who was also a very heavy buyer, had been saved $12.50; and when the government was saved under that policy, the taxpayer of course also saved. So great were the benefits that only blind adherence to the ideology of private

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
enterprise can account for the removal of these beneficial controls at a time when postwar inflation was upon us. In spite of all the gibes levelled against us by our political opponents and some sections of the press, our determined stand against the removal of beneficial controls and subsidies has been thoroughly vindicated-and, may I say, unfortunately vindicated-by the results.
So far I have dealt with the increased prices of basic foods, but tire effect of the prohibition or curtailment of other necessities will further increase the cost of living. Drastic cuts in the importation of textiles, particularly those which enter into the manufacture of overalls, denims for example, children's clothing and the cheaper grades of cloths and dress goods, will send prices up sharply. The promised effect of tariff reductions will not lighten the burden in this time of rising prices when we need relief. The prohibition of the importation of luxury goods from the United States because of the dollar shortage is intelligible but the prohibtion or the adoption of quotas in the importation of goods from sterling areas at this time is incomprehensible.
We are told that this is because w-e are bound by the non-discriminatory provisions of the Geneva tariff agreements which become effective on January 1 next. But there is an escape clause in this agreement which people seem to have overlooked, designed surely to meet an emergency like our own. I believe it is under section 14, but I did not make a note of it. We have until at least the first of January, 1949, before we need to apply the non-discrimination provisions. I say, at least until that date, because under certain circumstances that time can be further extended.
Why then are we prohibiting the importation of automobiles and other goods from the United Kingdom when she needs our food and we need her goods? It simply does not make sense. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the light of what I have said, I wish to move an amendment to the amendment that was moved last evening. I move:
That the following words be inserted in the amendment, after the word "motion" and before the word "we":
This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to use the powers provided by parliament to control prices, and by their actions have caused alarming increases in the cost of living and a dangerous lowering of the living standards of the Canadian people.
The crisis has jolted the government into action for the planned utilization of our resources. Planning may be good or it may be ill; it depends' on the purpose of- the plan. As outlined, the government's policy will, I believe, place our country more completely under the control of those monopolies and price-fixers who have exploited our people and our resources for generations. Such a plan must be resisted; for, taken in conjunction with prohibitions and price controls, it will deliver us lock, stock and barrel into the hands of the profiteer and the domestic exploiters, who have been exploiting the country for years. Moreover, it may have the further effect of delivering our economy more completely into the hands of big business and big industry than ever the old-fashioned Tory policies would have done.
If we are going to develop our resources as we should, then it should be done under public ownership and public control in the interests and for the welfare of the Canadian people. No other policy will meet the needs of our time or be sufficient. The cost of living has been going up for the past eighteen months. In the last few months it has been going up faster and faster, and in the next few months it will go up faster still. It has now reached the point where practically all the wage increase which the Canadian workers have gained since the spring of 1946 has been wiped out. At the same time profits are reaching new highs. The Nesbitt-Thomson dividend index, the oldest index in Canada, indicates a twenty per cent increase in profits over last year's figures, and last year's profits were the highest on record.
As it is, die government's policies have played into the hands of the profit-taking organizations in the past year to an almost incredible extent. It is all very well for the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) to go on the radio and describe such a statement in unparliamentary language as "a large lie." Let him or anyone else in this house deny the figures published recently by the Financial Post in its survey of corporate securities, 1947, which indicate the progressive rise in the profits of many essential industries. I have in my hand profit statements in dollars taken from the Financial Post of November 15, 1947. From the Financial Post survey of corporate securities-I shall not weary the house with a long list-I shall pick out a few. If the house desires I shall put the whole list on the record.
