That is an interjection that is surely a very feeble attempt to be funny.
It is a good one.

Only a feeble attempt to meet the charge that the friends of my hon. friends are making profits out of a policy that they have so long advocated.

Who is benefiting by the removal of these controls? Not the workers whose wage increases have not kept pace with prices; not the salary employees who remain an unorganized and exploited group in our society; certainly not the veteran whose gratuity and subsistence allowance at university dwindles, or who cannot find a home, or if he does, he pays through the nose for it; not the pensioner, whether of the first or second war, or any other form of pensioner whose meagre

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
gratuity buys less and less; not the underpaid civil servants whose average salaries are a national disgrace, and a disgrace to this house; not the person on a fixed income who saved and planned for the rainy day and invested in government or victory bonds-not any of these, but most of all the exploiters, the gamblers on the grain exchange who financed the Trestrails, the Gladstone Murrays, and who succeeded in defeating the people's candidates at the polls in 1945. They are tire beneficiaries of the mounting prices and the exploitation of the producers of this land, whether they farm, work in factories, mines or forests, go down to the sea in ships, or perform any other useful service in our society.
My time does not permit me to deal with the position of the wheat growers, except to say this. When the agreement was before this house, speaking on behalf of this group I made it clear that we supported the agreement with the understanding that I have already placed on the record this afternoon. We demanded that out of the consolidated revenue of Canada compensatory adjustments should be made if government policy allowed the costs of production to rise. We did not criticize it because the government's policy was a desertion of a low wheat price policy-
And then vote for it.

And then, incidentally, vote for it. Wre supported it because we wanted parity prices and a stabilized market. Today there is no parity and an uncertain market due to government action in removing the controls except for those on certain farm commodities, the principal one of which is wheat.
In conclusion I want to say that this is no time for half measures. I therefore want to place before this house and the government the following proposals:
1.	We ask for the re-imposition at the earliest possible date of price controls on all the basic necessities of life: food, clothing and fuel.
2.	The renewal of the subsidies on milk, butter, bread, feed grains, cotton and wool.
3.	The closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange and the elimination of all speculation in foods.
4.	Reconstruction of the wartime prices and trade board in such a manner that it can adequately administer the price controls.
5.	Continuation of the excess profits tax after December 31, 1947.
When I say "the excess profits tax" 1 realize that some changes must be made in the tax because it was a rough and ready war measure, and it should be re-considered in the light of the circumstances we now face.
6.	The rationing, if necessary, of any essential commodity which is in such short supply that some Canadians may not get their minimum share.
This is what we ask; this is what we have been asking, and, Mr. Speaker, I believe this is what the people of this country are asking at the present time. In countries where they have retained price control-and I have the figures in my hand-the cost of living has not risen, or has risen only slightly.
What a living they are getting!
What is the hon. member doing to help them?
Quite right; and what a living they are getting!
1 produce a lot more food than the hon. gentleman.

What a living they are getting! When we say that, we condemn ourselves for our self-satisfaction in the midst of a starving world.
When the Minister of Agriculture came back from Great Britain, he said that in spite of their austerity and their shortages the children of Britain were looking well fed. I do not think that the Minister of Agriculture should have left it just where he did, because he conveypd the wrong impression to the country, if I may say so, and did some harm to the cause in which I am sure he as well as the rest of us are interested. But I would point out that the reason these children are better than they ever were is that they are drinking more fluid milk than ever before in their history. Today every child in Britain gets his ration of milk whether he can pay for it or not. Every child is entitled to a free nourishing mid-day meal.
The outcry we hear from the kind of people who support my hon. friends to the right is because those who once got too much are now getting just a little too little, but that third or that half of the population of Great Britain who always got too little are now getting almost enough, but not quite enough. That is the reason for the outcry of the well-to-do and the wealthy today. The present policy in Great Britain, as in some other countries, is to redistribute the wealth of the nation so that all may receive a share at prices they can pay. In Great Britain butter
Does the hon. member know that Mr. Paul-Henri Spaak, Prime Minister of Belgium, is a socialist Prime Minister?

Yes, but he has not introduced
socialism.
Yes, a number of socialist principles.

Not a socialist principle. To continue the quotation:
Belgium did not take chances on vast complicated experiments like nationalization and socialization in meeting her post-war living problems and rising from the disaster of the German conquest and German occupation. Belgium decided on only one thing-the need to work and get well after the war. Belgium is really working and is paying the people to work. Presumbaly that is why they are working. The result is phenomenal. Belgium, you know, has little more to go on than England. There are the same fundamental limitations, amazingly similar, in Belgium and England, when you stop to think about it. Like England, Belgium lives on her coal-and must live on her coal. She, too, has practically no other natural resources-no oil, timber, iron ore, bauxite, water power-just coal. Belgium must dig coal to live-must export products made from coal in order to import foods and raw material. 'Like England her entire economy is rooted in her coal mines.
And, Mr. Speaker, you do not find Belgium today carrying coals to Newcastle at the rate of 340,000 tons a month, as they are doing in England.
Belgium's African colonies are valuable, but not a fraction as valuable as England's. She has only a small merchant fleet. Yet while England faces one economic crisis after another today, Belgium's industries are humming, her people have more food than any country in western Europe, outside Switzerland and Scandinavia. Her stores are full of merchandise from all over the wrorld. Her export trade is growing by leaps and bounds.
As David Perlman wrote in a recent survey:
"Belgian leaders are convinced they have found the one recovery policy that pays off. They point to other European countries where they say 'tight government check-reins on individual initiative and on business are slowing down production, keeping supplies off the market and widening the gap between upward moving incomes and prices. 'Consistently and as rapidly as possible the Belgians have restored liberty to individual action in sector after sector of this nation's economic life."
While twenty per cent of the French population serve in non-productive places in government bureaux and must be carried by the productive workers of the nation and work at the taxpayers' expense-and while ten per cent of the British people work for the British government today, practically nobody in Belgium works for the Belgian government. Instead the Belgians are working for themselves. They get the results of their labour in better living, instead of having it drained off in government overhead and confusion. Accordingly, they are rebuilding this country. Belgium's coal production fell as low as twenty-five per cent of capacity at the end of the war under German occupation-lower than England's erer fell. Bel-
The Address-Mr. Low

gium's mining machinery is older than England's. Yet Belgium is producing coal up to ninety per cent of capacity today, while England's production remains far lower than pre-war.
Belgium didn't nationalize her coal mines. Belgium did not throw her economic problems into polities. She stuck with an incentive system and free management. And that is the basic answer.
Socialism means mismanagement. Mismanagement means lower living standards for average people. Belgium has avoided this-England has not. The beneficial results spread all through national activities here and make this country 'the envy of all neighbours except Switzerland where a similar program was followed. Belgium's thirteen principal industries are running at 107 per cent of pre-war production. A fine record, my friends, for a country deep in the heart of wartorn Europe! Her steel industry is not threatened by nationalization. Under private management the Belgian public is investing millions in personal savings toward modernization of the steel mills. Reinvestment of funds here, by the public as a whole, in Belgium's own enterprises is at a faster rate than at any time since before the war.
Nothing like that is happening in England. Britons who have saved any money, wage earners and others who have been thrifty, are not putting their money into the British steel industry. They don't know when the mills will be nationalized by the government; so the whole investment flow on the British isles dries up, and the British equipment goes from bad to worse. Here, on the other hand. Belgium's steel output is well above par. In fact, Belgium is exporting steel to England!
Again in contrast with hard-pressed Great Britain, where the socialist labour government experiment casts the same kind of pall over textile rehabilitation as over steel, Belgium's textile industry is pushing production upward month by month. Nearly half of the nation's cotton doth is sold abroad. The exports are now paying for imports from all corners of the world. East month Belgium's exports of all kinds were three times as great as her pre-war average and nearly equalled her imports, including the stock piles and the new machinery Belgium had 'to buy and which she paid for. There is no shortage of American dollars because she is making and selling the goods that create American dollar credit.
Meanwhile there is no program here for austerity living either. Along with Switzerland, the living conditions in Belgium approach those in our own country-in food and clothes and everything else. There is a good relationship between wages and prices.
Here, then, is a European nation at work- co-operating, producing, living, growing, prospering. Attacked, blitzed, battered and occupied by the Germans, Belgium nevertheless has been wise in its recovery-hard-working enough and eager enough to recover through its own self help under a system of free enterprise.
If further evidence is needed, there is plenty of it available. I shall refer briefly to an article which appeared in the issue of Time for September 22. If anyone wishes some really interesting reading I suggest that he get that issue and consider it caiefully. At

page 24 under the heading "Planned Agriculture", we find that the foreign correspondent of that magazine paints a picture of the bureaucratic set-up in England's agriculture today.
What country'?

Great Britain. He states:
Early one morning last week, Farmer Frederick Henry Dennis-
And hon. members will notice that this correspondent gives names, places, times and ages. I have watched carefully since that day to find out if those facts have ever been refuted, and I have seen no effort whatever made to refute them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not interrupt the hon. member a moment ago when he read a long extract, but I would remind him that it is not in order to read long extracts from newspapers
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order-and I would ask him not to read long extracts.
From what is the hon. member quoting?
Time magazine.
Who gave the orders?

The orders came from a board composed of county agriculturists, and the ministry of agriculture which had at its head the Right Hon. Tom Williams who never had a bunion any place except where it was caused by sitting on a chair. He never saw a plow in his life.
If the local agricultural committee decided that, there must have been something more behind it.

There was. Just one other point in connection' with this. The article says that the agricultural committee can prosecute a farmer for disobeying crop "advice" as it is called. Our C.C.F. friends, with their planned agriculture and 'with their planned economy, are only going to give "advice", but that advice will be made into law and when the law is laid down, people must obey it or be prosecuted before the courts. I quote briefly from the article as follows:
The committee might have ordered Farmer Dennis to plow in his buckwheat while it was green. But time passed and the committee did nothing. Instead it let the buckwheat ripen. Then it acted. Obviously the committee had bungled.
And again:
Meanwhile, Farmer Dennis faced prosecution, and hungry Britons would go without several thousand meals which the plowed-in grain could have provided in the form of ham, pork or chicken.
If any better picture could be obtained of so called "planned agriculture" and "planned economy" I should like to see it.
A dumping policy.

My friends the socialists are very adept in dealing in slogans, but may I remind them that slogans never put bread upon the tables of hungry people. Slogans have never at any time filled coal bins with coal, and slogans have never at any time provided new houses in place of old ones.
Vote for $25 a month.

Let me suggest to the hon. lady member that if she had voted for $25 a month she would not have been forced to share the scarcity there is today. If other countries under socialist administrations had voted for $25 a month they would not have the scarcities they have today.
And did not get it.

I am quite ready to admit that there is much that we can learn from the countries of Europe, but in my judgment the greatest lesson that we in Canada can learn is not to make the same mistakes that they have been making in countries under socialist governments, particularly the mistake of thinking that there is any substitute for personal initiative and hard work and reward to the individual man and woman for individual accomplishments. I say that the freedom of opportunity for individuals is rapidly being lost to many people in Europe through the creeping paralysis of both socialism and communism.
I conclude my reference to this part of what has been said by declaring that it is my firm opinion and deep conviction that socialism is bound to fail everywhere because it is so radically contrary to economic truth, to law and to human nature. Human nature will always rebel against regimentation, but it will always respond to the proper inducement.
During the recess between the sessions I travelled extensively throughout western Canada and I found there widespread dismay about the skyrocketing costs of living. It was perfectly clear that the white collar class and unorganized labour were suffering and finding it most difficult to pay their way out of current earnings. They were dipping into their savings and liquidating their few bonds in order to make ends meet. Old age pensioners and veteran pensioners and their dependents are in many cases suffering from privation. Throughout the whole of Canada these people are finding that their pensions, which were all too inadequate to begin with, have shrunken to a point where they are no more than 70 per cent of their original value.
Yet these same people are still expected to carry a tax load which was burdensome even when the cost of living index was below 125. The latest figures I have been able to obtain indicate that the cost of living now stands at a figure higher than 145, and many predict that it will exceed 150, and that soon. The condition of organized labour is not quite so bad, but their predicament is bad enough.
Every thinking person is asking why this government has not taken action before this to remedy the whole situation. Quite clearly some relief should have been provided months ago, before things got out of hand. People generally are becoming aroused over the fact that the figures show that the government is piling up a surplus which promises to reach perhaps $700 million by the end of the fiscal year, and yet no move has been made to lighten the onerous tax burden and to prevent
The Address-Mr. Low

the ever-spiraling and increasing cost of living, either through the use of subsidies or compensated price discounts.
I know that prices in Canada are affected to some extent by prices in the United States, and that therefore considerable upward pressure in living costs is to be expected because of our proximity to the great republic to the south, but that fact does not excuse this government for failing to tackle the thing which is one of the major root causes of high living costs. I refer to hidden or indirect taxation. This year this government is taking from the people of Canada $1,100 million in sales, excise, turnover, processing and other indirect taxes. All of this has the effect of pushing the cost of living higher because these taxes are added to costs at different levels of production and processing. This same type of legalized robbery also affects adversely Canada's trading position and reduces materially the help we can extend to European countries to get back on their own feet. Surely, with a surplus of income over expenditure rising to three-quarters of a billion dollars, the government is going to find it impossible to explain satisfactorily to the people of Canada why some of that surplus has not been used to grant relief to the people in the form of tax reductions which would offset to some extent the high living cost. I am not surprised that I never hear from my socialist friends any suggestion that taxes be reduced because they believe in taxation; they want taxation to sta)' on.
Again, Canadians from coast to coast will not forget that the government proceded with indecent haste to abolish subsidies, which for many months had been the most effective means of price control. The Social Credit group in this house consistently urged and voted for the retention of subsidies. As a matter of fact we have taken the position that subsidies, together with the compensated price discount, which was so successful in milk price control during the war, must become a permanent feature of our national economy in the future if we.are to avoid a repetition of the hungry thirties and such crises as Canada now faces with skyrocketing prices.

Does the hon. member propose the maintenance of price subsidies without price control?
, Mr. LOW: They could not possibly be maintained-*
Without price control?
Surely.
What kind of price control does the hon. member propose?
The kind of control that is exercised through the compensated price discount and the payment of subsidies.
The payment of subsidies is not in itself price control.

I did not say it was. I cannot stop at this moment to deal with the point but one of my colleagues at a later stage in this debate will take time to make abundantly clear what is meant by the compensated price discount plus the subsidy.
It is evident, Mr. Speaker, that this government has shamefully mismanaged the economy of this country by kicking out subsidies and declaring that they have no place in Liberal policy. At the same time their precipitate and unreasoned action has endangered the health of millions of our citizens who now find that they cannot afford to buy sufficient milk and fresh fruits and vegetables to maintain their diet at a healthful level. The government cannot be excused on the ground that the people were demanding the removal of subsidies and price controls. The overwhelming majority of the members of this house, I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, declared their opposition to the removal of the milk subsidy in particular, and such others as were necessary to hold consumer prices in control; and the Social Credit group in this house did all in their power to preserve them at all costs.
In my travels this summer and autumn I talked to hundreds of farmers and listened to their problems and their difficulties. The farmers of the west generally are angry, and very angry, at the treatment they have received from this government. Not only that, but I found much discouragement amongst them which has affected adversely their will to produce. That is a serious situation. They say that the livestock situation as a result of government policy, or rather lack of policy, is little short of a national calamity, and I believe that. In the first place, the farmers as a class have been left to bear the major portion of the burden of assistance which Canada has given to the United Kingdom. In the main the farmers favour stabilization of farm income but, Mr. Speaker, they also think they are entitled to some reasonable stabilization of farm outgo. They think that the assistance granted to Britain by way of lower than world wheat prices for Canadian wheat should have been carried by all the people of Canada. We in this corner most certainly agree with them.

The Address-Mr. Low
We have consistently urged in past sessions the use of the compensated price discount to keep the prices of things the farmers have to buy in better relationship with the world prices of the products they have to sell. We have also consistently advocated the use of subsidies from the national treasury to bring the contract price of wheat and of livestock products up to world price levels. Action of this kind would have spread the cost of aid to Britain over the merchant, the professional men, organized and unorganized labour and industry as well as the farmers. The farmers do not mind carrying their share, but they will not soon forget that in the government's gamble with their wheat, they are the ones who thus far have had to take the burden of the losses.
I have already said that the livestock situation has become a national calamity. I received a day or two ago a telegram, amongst manj' telegrams and letters that have come to me, from the Fairview board of trade. Fairview is right in the midst of what I consider to be the greatest productive farming area in all Canada, the Peace River country. The Fairview board of trade calls the present livestock situation a national calamity, and they demand the action I shall shortly suggest, to rectify it.
The action of the government, in removing coarse grains ceilings, and doing it right in the middle of the marketing season, has thrown the whole Canadian livestock industry into utter confusion. How in the wide world [DOT]the government can possibly justify such stupidity is much more than farmers or anyone else can possibly understand. Something has to be done at once to correct the adverse effect which the government's policies have had on farm production. I fear it will take years, Mr. Speaker, to restore confidence amongst farmers generally; and positive, well-founded inducements will have to be held up to them before incentive to all-out production can be established again. But it can be accomplished by timely and proper action, action which will certainly have to be taken at once. It is a shameful and tragic thing that just now when the health, happiness, and well-being, perhaps even the very lives of millions of people depend upon our production of foodstuffs, government policies should be demoralizing agriculture and denying these people the opportunity to consume our foodstuffs.
Last night I listened attentively to the address of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and I felt with him some of the gravity of the world situation. I was able to get a glimpse of the grave world situation also in my experience at the United Nations
Assembly last autumn. I was grateful for the opportunity to go down to Lake Success and see for myself what went on there. I should like to spend some time this afternoon in giving some of my impressions but I shall have to refrain because my time is rapidly passing. Perhaps another opportunity will be afforded for me to do that. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that grave as is the world situation as painted by the Prime Minister last night, it certainly cannot be blamed for all of the crises now facing our country. Government policy must take its share and its rightful share of the responsibility for the crises we do face.
To deal with the dollar crisis just for a moment, it is our belief that the hasty action of the government in bringing the Canadian dollar to parity with the United States dollar has contributed as much as any other reason to the rapid dwindling of our dollar reserves, and to the impasse we have now reached. On the basis of that advice alone, the economic illiterates-for there is no other name for them-and pure theorists who somehow have been fastened on this government as economic and financial advisers, should be dismissed and sent back to the London School of Economics where they can give full play to the puerile effusions of their mentalities of scarcity.
I wish to remind the house that Social Creditere during recent years have consistently warned against bringing the Canadian dollar to parity with that of our neighbours across the line, so long as we were experiencing an adverse balance of trade. We have pointed out what the inevitable effects would be. I wish to quote from page 3045 of Hansard of July 2, 1946, what the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) said:
But on every occasion this matter has come up in the house, I have objected to the suggestion that the Canadian dollar should be placed on a parity with the United States dollar. My reason for taking that position is this: if that parity is established, either Canadian exporters will receive ten per cent less for their exports or the foreign purchasers will pay ten per cent more. In either case, Canadian exports will be discouraged; and in view of the fact that the United States is our main, or, perhaps I should say our only, creditor, the present need is to encourage our exports to that country rather than the reverse.
Mr. Speaker, our warning went unheeded just as did our warning about Bretton Woods in 1945. I say that if the government had listened to our arguments on both subjects they could have kept themselves out of a great deal of serious trouble and the Canadian public today might not be faced with an austerity program. Of course, austerity has become fashionable and Canada could hardly be expected to stay out of the swim when

The Address-Mr. Low
one realizes the amount of socialistic advice which the Canadian government has been receiving.
However, Mr. Speaker, now that we are in the mess we feel that as one means of correcting the whole situation we must support the government's temporary restriction of imports from the United States, especially of luxury goods. But we register very strong objections to limiting importations of citrous fruits and fresh vegetables. The Canadian people need these things to prevent the impairment of their health through our long, cold winter. We also register the strongest objection to the very heavy excise taxes on many things, domestic as well as imported, which have come to be looked upon as necessities of life in this day.
It must be evident to everyone that these taxes will have a great inflationary effect upon our economy in Canada, a thing we have been trying to avoid. If the main purpose of the government is to use these taxes to drain off purchasing power so as to minimize inflation, it seems a peculiar way to go about it using inflation to fight inflation. As one newspaperman put it, that is like creating chaos to meet crisis. I shall shortly suggest a much better way of draining off surplus purchasing power.
It appears that this government is beginning to realize that the sins of omission of past governments of Canada are catching up with them. When one examines the records of imports from the United States, it becomes plain that another factor contributing to the dollar shortage is the wilful neglect on the part of past administrations to develop our industries and resources right here in Canada.
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he has spoken for forty minutes.
Go ahead.

I promise I will not take much longer. I want to refer for a moment to some figures that show the total amount of money spent for various items in the United States during the year 1946. Canada purchased from the United States in that year coal to the value of $119,453,000. That required United States currency. In that year we also purchased petroleum and petroleum products to the value of $82,757,000; automobiles to the value of $31,120,000; sugar from the United States and other dollar countries to the value of $28 million in round figures; a total in those four items of $261,331,000. And then we wonder why it is that we are running into a dollar crisis! Such figures indicate that to a very great extent, in the essentials of living, Canada is dependent upon the United States;

and I say to you, sir, that such dependence upon uncertain sources, and they are very often uncertain, puts Canada in a dangerously weak position in times of crises. We should now be supplying many of them from our own resources. We can supply them if we develop our country as it should be.
I am pleased to note the government's intention to do something about correcting this situation, and particularly the whole dangerous situation of being utterly dependent, in the essentials of living, upon other countries. I hope that the program of the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) will be started at a -wartime tempo, to make Canada as nearly self-sufficient in the essentials of living as it is possible to make it. Let me warn him, however, not to expect success unless his program is based upon inducement and incentive rather than upon compulsion and high-handed government intervention in business. He must not live in the past with regard to a measure of economic nationalism.
Too many of our government people in past years have been completely afraid of any form of economic nationalism. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that any program of industrialization in Canada, to be successful, must be a dynamic one, designed to make Canada strong and independent. The necessity of becoming strong and independent is forcing every country, through the events of the present day, into economic nationalism more or less complete.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I believe that with the right kind of leadership and with a proper program of objectives, Canada can pull out of the bad situation she is in at present, and at the same time she can be enabled to extend substantial help to other less fortunate countries, notably Britain. I am going to propose a five-point program which I feel is the kind we must follow if we are to achieve the results we want in this respect.
My proposal is based upon the principle that whatever is physically possible and desirable can and should be made financially possible. I am glad to note that there is growing recognition of this principle which Social Crediters for twenty-six years have kept before the people of the world to make them conscious of the utter absurdities that have been demonstrated by a so-called financial system that breeds debt, scarcity, suffering and war.
I note with satisfaction that the president of the Canadian federation of agriculture, Mr. Hannam, recognizes the profound truth that is bound up in that principle. He so stated a few days ago. The starting point in our attack on the problem arising from the crisis now facing us has to be on the real bottleneck, and that bottleneck, I suggest, is Britain's inability to

The Address-Mr. Abbott
get to her underfed people the abundance of foodstuffs and other things which Canada can produce.
That whole preposterous situation arises from, and revolves around the fact that dollars are not available to Britain with which she can make necessary purchases in Canada. I say, then, why not begin our program by making those dollars available?
My first point therefore is this-a food-for-Britain loan. The idea is not by any means original. I must give credit to the Ottawa Citizen for reminding me that this is the right place to start. The government should go to the people of Canada with a national drive to raise-say-$2 billion to lend to Britain for food and other supplies from Canada. Bank reports show that as of August 1947 total deposits amounted to more than $7 billion; therefore there is plenty of money available. That would accomplish two things.
(a)	It would drain off redundant purchasing power and help to offset inflation in Canada, thus obviating the necessity of the new excise taxes, if any such necessity exists.
(b)	It would provide at once a market for Canada's production, and provide incentive for all-out efforts in our country.
2.	Call for an all-out agricultural production program.
In this connection, set about restoring confidence among farmers, and provide incentive and inducement, by:
(a)	Immediate tax reduction, direct and hidden.
(b)	Subsidies from the national treasury to bring wheat contract price up to world price.
(c)	Boost livestock returns by bonus or subsidy.
(d)	Compensated price discounts to consumers as a means of bringing cost of living under control.
3.	Introduce at wartime speed and urgency a national program of industrialization, with the object of making Canada as nearly selfsufficient as possible in the essentials of living. In launching such a program, we must avoid dictatorial methods, and rely upon proper inducements rather than on compulsion.
4.	Adopt a balanced trade policy based upon mutual benefit and contracredits, instead of upon the most-favoured-nation clause and Bretton Woods, about which we have warned this house.
We like and admire our good friends and neighbours to the south of us, but somehow United States traders and commercial interests must be brought to understand that the aggressive insistence by their country upon trade agreements based upon the most-favourednation clause, is one of the greatest reasons
for the present chaotic condition of world trade; for much of the fear of the mighty United States now manifest throughout the world; and for the alarming rate at which the British commonwealth is being dissolved.
5.	An immediate move to set our own house in apple-pie order: so as to ensure that every Canadian is made secure in his own rights and freedoms, which includes freedom to consume. Without going into further details in this regard, I should like to commend to you a nine-point program currently being circulated amongst Ontario members of this house by the Ontario social credit league.
All these things are physically possible. They must be made financially possible. I should like to say something about the Geneva trade agreements, but my time has more than expired. I shall therefore content myself to wait until these things are brought before the house to make any further presentation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some diffidence to take part in this debate because I have an idea that over the next ten days or two weeks I may have to do rather more than my share of talking in this house. My apprehensions in that regard are more than borne out by the number of questions that were fired at me on the orders of the day today. However, there have been brought out in the course of the remarks of the speakers who have preceded me some points which I think call for some answer at this time on behalf of the government.
Before I do that, though, I wish to join with others in extending to the mover and the seconder of the address my most sincere congratulations on the performance which they put on, as to both form and content. In the manner of delivery both their addresses were excellent, and if I may interject a personal note, I think both of them were very generous and complimentary in their references to myself.
Coming now to the remarks which were made by the leader of the opposition, (Mr. Bracken), the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) and the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low), may I say that I do not intend to spend a great deal of time in dealing with the remarks made by the leader of the official opposition. He spent a considerable portion of his time in dealing with matters which relate more particularly to the emergency program, the dollar conservation program, and I think this can be mo'e properly discussed when the measures are introduced to put these proposals into effect. There were,
The Address-Mr. Abbott
Will the minister permit one question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Will the minister say why this subsidy was not taken off on August 1, at the start of the marketing year, if it was to come off?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I will answer that quickly. It was not taken off on Auugst 1 because meat ceilings were not to be taken off until September 15. It was originally intended that the meat ceilings would be taken off on September 15 when the last major move in the decontrol program was made. At that time unfortunately the meat strike was on and the subsidy was paid for the time being, while the meat strike was in process of settlement. I do not believe that the great majority either of feeders or of growers ever thought the subsidy would be continued during the coming crop year.
I think the minister misunderstood me.
Sit down.

The minister is quite willing to answer if his supporters are not. I asked about the crop year which commenced on August 1. The strike began on September 12. The marketing year commenced on August 1. That is where the confusion has arisen among the producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will concede to my hon. friend that there may have been some confusion in the minds of some producers. I make this statement again. The great majority of the producers were satisfied that this subsidy was not to be continued during the coming year. I make the assertion here that I do not believe this is a proper type of subsidy. If you are paying a subsidy at any time, that subsidy should not be paid to one class of producer while you discriminate against another class; and I doubt if my hon. friend would want to sustain that thesis in western Canada.

The Address-Mr. Abbott
I have always advocated that on the floor of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I made the point that this was a temporary subsidy to enable price ceilings to be maintained on meat and dairy products. That- is all I have to say about the subsidy question. I wanted to make clear to the house the history of the subsidy, to show that it was only introduced last March and was never intended to be permanent. It was unfortunate that the discontinuance of the subsidy should have coincided with a partial crop failure in eastern Canada, but that was one of those things that sometimes happen and certainly it was something over which the government had no control.
The second point I wish to refer to, arising out of the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, was one I had anticipated; that is, his criticism of the action of the government in June, 1946, in revaluing the Canadian dollar and bringing it to parity from a discount of ten per cent, together with his further suggestion that it should be devalued again. The same point was raised by my hon. friend the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low). When that action was taken in June of 1946 I do not recall that the leader of the opposition or any member of the Progressive Conservative party rose in his place to object to it. If they did I shall be glad to stand corrected, but I think I am right. It is quite true, as the hon. member for Peace River says, that his party did object. However, I say to this house now, as my predecessor, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) said in June, 1946, when that action was taken, that it was a step which was fully justified, one which was in the interests of the Canadian people, and one which the government has never regretted having taken.
What would have been the result over the last twelve or eighteen months if that action had not been taken? Our imports from the United States during the past year have run something in the order of $2,000 million. It would have meant that from our exchange reserves we would have paid out some $200 million more than we have paid out. It may be urged by hon. gentlemen opposite that we would not have bought as much in the United States if our dollar had been at a discount of ten per cent. Let me make this suggestion, as I did in my radio broadcast. Since June of 1946 the average price of our imports from the United States has risen forty per cent, and our imports have not diminished; they have increased. If any hon. member will suggest to me that an extra ten per cent would have slowed down those
imports I am afraid he is less intelligent than I give hon. members of this house credit for being. That is the position, Mr. Speaker, and we cannot get away from it. The average price of our imports has risen forty per cent, and they have not diminished; they have increased. On the other hand, by bringing our dollar to parity we have expended from our reserves some $200 million less than otherwise we would have spent. Currency depreciation is a device which may be resorted to, and which it may be desirable to resort to, if the value, either internal or external, of one's currency is above its real purchasing power; but that is not the case with respect to the Canadian dollar. We are not handicapped in a single export market of the world because our dollar is at par with the United States dollar. We are not losing a single sale in that market because our prices are too high. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in suggesting that we devalue the Canadian dollar now, said at page 58 of Hansard of yesterday:
The drain of dollars has been so great that the amount of depreciation permitted within the Bretton Woods agreement would not be sufficient to cure the worsened situation, but it would do something.
It certainly would do something. One of the things it would do would be to put immediately a ten per cent tariff right across the board on everything we import from the United States. It would add ten per cent to the price of the coal we import. It would add ten per cent to the price of the petroleum and gasoline we import. It would add ten per cent to the cost of the steel we import. It would add ten per cent to the cost of the thousand and one things we bring into this country. That is what it would do. I challenge anyone to contradict successfully that statement.
Would you make your comparison on balance rather than just on what we spend? Would they not spend more with us if their dollar was worth $1.10?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would not get any more in the United States. We would not sell any more. We would sell the same quantity of goods.
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We rvould not bring in more United States dollars. We are selling every ton of newsprint we can produce; it is being sold in the United States market at a price in United States dollars. The only way we would get more money for newsprint in the United States would be to take that
The Address-Mr. Abbott

newsprint from Britain, or to take it from somewhere else, perhaps from our own newspapers; but we would not get any more dollars. We would still get the $90 or $100 a ton, whatever it may be. It is true that the newspaper producer would get, in Canadian dollars, $10 more than he is getting now. Any exchange depreciation gives a benefit to the individual importer, but it does not benefit the country as a whole. That is the point I make.
Mr. COCIvERAM: Would the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I like to answer questions; there is nothing I like better.
Does the minister not think that if our dollar were at a discount of ten per cent United States capital would once more flow into this country for investment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a matter of opinion. If United States capital came into this country and was invested permanently in plants, in bricks and mortar, I would welcome it. But if it came into the country to buy short-term securities or to buy stocks and bonds in the hope of making a quick speculative profit in the event of the dollar being brought up to parity again, then I say we do not want that kind of investment.
I am delighted that this question has been raised. I knew it would be, and I am glad to deal with it now. Another result of the suggestion of my hon. friend would be to make it more difficult for Britain, France, Czechoslovakia and other countries to sell their goods in this country. I can tell hon. members that in some of those countries costs are already so high that in some lines they have difficulty meeting price competition in this country. If by our own action we were to add, let us say, ten per cent or fifteen per cent or whatever you like to their costs, we would certainly not help them balance their trade with Canada.
I am perfectly well aware that in this country there is a school of thought that wants to take off exchange controls and let things rip. I quite realize that; but I am not one of that school. I say the policy the government has followed to date with respect to the value of the Canadian dollar is a sound policy and one that is in the interests of the Canadian people.
How do you explain the plight we are in now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to that plight business in a moment; I will come to the references to Jeremiah and all the rest of it.
[Mr. Abbott.1
After all, facts are facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then my hon. friend the leader of the opposition made another point with which I wish to deal. At page 59 of Hansard of yesterday he said:
The government's policies froze farmers' prices at the top and allowed the cost of the farmers' business to increase in some cases by nearly fifty per cent overnight.
I want to place some figures on record as to this question of farmers' costs and prices. These are the official figures of the dominion bureau of statistics.
The farmers must be awfully stupid if they do not know their own costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Farmers are not the only people who perhaps are not as intelligent as they may think. In 1939, at the outbreak of war, the index of farm prices stood at 84-3. Today, or at the last date available, which would be within the last two or three weeks, the index of farm prices stands at 181-3, or a rise of 115-1 per cent. That is on farm prices. During the same period general wholesale prices rose from 93-2 to 179-5, or 92-6 per cent, and the cost of living index from 100-8 to 143-6 or 42-5 per cent.
On these figures I think it is pretty hard to sustain the thesis that the farmers have not had a fair increase in prices. They have had the biggest; but I do not suggest it is unfair, for this reason, that farm prices before 1939 were depressed. They were unduly depressed. And I think the industrial section of the economy was being subsidized, if I may use that word, or was being benefited at the expense of the agricultural section.
That balance has been redressed. But I will not admit that the farmers have not had their fair share of increases in prices.
Try to prove that to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a matter of fact the food index, as hon. members know, has risen far more than any other element in the cost of living.
We were talking about feed prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You make your speech when you get a chance. I am sure it will be a dandy.

When do we get the chance? We cannot have a chance; that is

The Address-Mr. Abbott
the trouble. Are you prepared to give us a chance? If you will let us have a chance, then that is all we are asking for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, my hon. friend does pretty well.

He talked all day
3'esterday.
And said nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is about all I have to say, concerning the remarks of the. leader of the opposition. As I say, he made a number of observations respecting the so-called emergency legislation which I believe I might more appropriately leave over until we are discussing that legislation. I cannot see any real purpose in taking the time of the house to have two debates on the same matter.
Jeremiah?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall refer to Jeremiah in my peroration.
Before the minister leaves farm prices-
Oh, oh,
Well, he said he was finished with the farm part of his speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said I was finished with the leader of the opposition.

Just a minute now. With respect to the lifting of the ceilings on oats and barley, will the minister state whether the producers who delivered those oats and 'barley will 'be reimbursed for the money they lost in connection with the ceiling?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not within my province to announce legislation that may be introduced. I will give my hon. friend the classic answer, that this is a matter of government policy and that it will be announced in due course.
I turn now to the remarks of the leader of the C.C.F. group. He answered a point made by the leader of the opposition with which I had intended to deal, namely, that we should leave enough in this country to prevent prices from going up, when he put the question to the leader of the opposition as to whether that hon. gentleman intended to take those quantities from the United Kingdom, or from where he intended to take them. I should think the answer to that is fairly self-evident.
With respect to the points raised by the leader of the C.C.F. group, I wish to deal, first, with his suggestion that we should
re-impose price ceilings. The way he put it was that we should re-impose over-all price ceilings on the basic necessities. I have forgotten his exact language, but I believe that is reasonably accurate. First, let me say that in persuing its program of orderly decontrol-
You mean chaos.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In continuing its policy of orderly decontrol, the government was carrying out its pledges to the electorate. May I say that whatever stand may be taken by some parties in the house, at least the Liberal party is consistent in that if it promises something when it goes to the country it carries out those promises.
That is the first reason we pursued an orderly decontrol policy. And, despite what may be said by some hon. members, it has been an orderly decontrol policy. I was interested to hear the leader of the opposition during the campaign in York-Sunbury refer to the disorderly decontrol policy. But when I recall what he and his supporters have been advising us to do, I did not pay too much attention to it, and neither did the electors of York-Sunbury. I think it will be generally agreed that the government did a pretty good job of price stabilization during the war. As a matter of fact the job was so well done that the government is now in danger of being damned by praise of its own virtuous actions, and by the argument that we should be able to do now what we were able to do during the war. I have been told that there is a tendency among generals to fight the last war instead of the war ahead. I think that is the tendency of those who are urging now that we can continue over-all price controls instead of a peacetime policy. While we welcome the commendation we have received with respect to our wartime price control policy, I suggest that it would be a serious mistake for anyone to believe that a policy which was appropriate under wartime conditions could 'be carried into effect successfully under peacetime conditions.
It will be recalled that when the government imposed its over-all price ceilings policy in November of 1941, in effect it froze prices at their then existing levels.
It is true that adjustments were made from time to time in those prices, particularly in the direction of allowing farm prices to rise. Subsidies were paid in order to increase the returns for certain essential products and to stabilize the cost of living. But, by and large, the ceiling which was observed until decontrol started was the ceiling which preserved the general structure of prices existing at the end of 1941.
The Address-Mr. Abbott

This stabilization of the price structure was of immeasurable value in maximizing the country's war effort; and I think if I had the responsibility of recommending a similar policy, again under wartime conditons-which God forbid-I would suggest that we should adopt a similar policy. Nevertheless I think every hon. member would agree that the structure of the prices which existed in 1941 was not suitable to the very much altered conditions and circumstances of 1947.
For example, I do not suppose anyone would seriously suggest that we should go back to 77-cent wheat, or that consumers should be permitted to continue buying their flour on the basis of 77-cent wheat by subsidizing the present price on that basis. Nor would it be reasonable for the government to subsidize raw cotton, which is an essential and is used in so many ways, down to the prices which were just about one-third of the prices which prevail today on the world market. Yet, just as soon as anomalies such as these are corrected, others begin to appear and it is necessary to have a complete readjustment to the realities of present-day conditions. Let me give an excellent example in connection with decontrol. One of the later things to be decontrolled was the charges for trucking services. On account of the fact that those charges enter largely into a number of things, we held the level on charges for trucking services until almost the end.
Well, I wish hon. members could have heard the bitter complaints from the trucking contractors. They came to us and said, "Everything we have to buy is going up in price. Gasoline is going up; the wages we have to pay are going up. The grease we have to buy has gone up, as has the cost of our vehicles." All these, they said, had increased. Then they said, "Yet, you do not let us charge more for our service."
That is an excellent example of how the fixing of a single price involves costs which spread out, throughout the economy. Someone will suggest, "Why not impose over-all price ceilings today? Why not start again in 1947 and impose the ceilings on 1947 prices?" Well, those who suggest such a policy have not worked out all its implications. In the first place, my belief is that over-all price control cannot be put into effect unless there is real and effective control over salaries and wages.
I am convinced1 that that is the case. I do not believe that those who favour the reimposition of price control would advocate such a policy. The control of salaries and wages is within the jurisdiction of the provinces today, and, I believe, properly so under our constitution as it exists.
Our experience during wartime leads us to the conclusion that price control is likely to

break down at vital spots unless the government is in a position to enforce its direction upon producers. There is no use in our saying to a manufacturer of textiles, "You have to sell shirts at X dollars per shirt", unless we are prepared to force him to do it. He will not produce shirts at $3 per shirt or whatever it is and go into bankruptcy as a result. What will he do? He will simply stop producing.
If you are going to enforce over-all price control of that kind you must be prepared to carry through and to impose directions upon producers. I am glad to say that during the war the government received widespread co-operation in carrying out some of its directives. Very seldom did we have to wield the big stick, but the authority was there. I think it would have to be there again if we are to introduce over-all price control.
Finally, the application of any form of general price control, particularly if it were accompanied by a roll-back of prices as is suggested in some quarters, would involve the allocation of scarce goods, rationing and so forth. I know that is what my hon. friends of the C.C.F. advocate. In short, let me emphasize this point. Any system of over-all price control involves over-all detailed direction of the Canadian economy.
Would the minister hazard a guess or estimate as to what the cost to the country would be if there were a rollback of prices?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And also what it would save?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is one of those calculations which it is almost impossible to make. Say there is a roll-back of prices of ten per cent. W'hat is the total value of goods and services? Would you then take ten per cent? Would you take ten per cent off the fellow who drives a truck? It is hard to know where to stop.
You can have an over-all price control and rationing system, but one point I should like to make is that Canada is one of the greatest trading nations in the world. We import and export more per capita than almost any other country in the world, and perhaps it is fair to say, more than any other country in the world. What does that mean? It means inevitably that we cannot have our price level too far away from world price levels. There is no use in our trying to fool ourselves about that.
I know that this appeal for over-all price ceilings and controls is a plausible one and has a great deal of popularity, but I for one am not going to indulge in what we used to call in the army, "trying to kid the troops". I say that unless this country is prepared to embark upon a completely controlled and completely

The Address-Mr. Abbott
directed economy, then we cannot go back in peacetime to over-all price ceilings. That is entirely apart from whatever our rights might be under the constitution as it exists.
I realize that there will be an opportunity later on to discuss this matter when the motion for an address to extend the powers for another period comes up, but I have attempted briefly to give the reasons why I believe it is impossible to reimpose over-all price ceilings in Canada. However, I do not want to leave the impression with the house or with the country that the government is prepared to adopt a hands-off policy, because it is not. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has indicated, we are going to ask parliament for a temporary extension of our authority.
Hon. members will have seen that certain proposals are pending before the United States congress for authority to impose some measure of control in that country. I am not going to go into the details, but inevitably any action that we take here must be influenced by what action is taken in the United States. The present intention of the government is, as hon. members know, to ask for an extension of the powers which now exist to impose and maintain price controls for a further period. I would hope that during that further period it will be possible for us to get a clearer idea of just what can be done in this field in the interests of the Canadian economy.
I should like to say just one more word on the question of price control. The charge was made by my hon. friend that the decontrol policy was dictated by what he referred to as vested interests. I deny that without any hesitation. It was not dictated by any group. It was a policy which we announced before the election. It was the policy which we believed was the only policy which could be enforced. It is the policy which we have carried out in accordance with our prearranged program, and I deny emphatically that it was dictated by any interest, vested or otherwise.
Another point which he raised was in connection with the new emergency measures. I only want to touch on this. He referred to what he termed the discriminatory clauses which prohibited things from coming in from the United Kingdom. I intend to discuss this in more detail when the measure is before the house. The United States in particular attaches great importance to the non-discrimination principle. While it possibly could not be called a fetish with them, it is a principle to which great importance is attached. The success of this emergency program and the smooth functioning of our economy depend
upon the whole-hearted co-operation of our friends to the south. That has been evidenced by their willingness to make us a loan of $300 million.
We wish as far as possible to make our program non-discriminatory, because I for one believe that that is a most desirable principle. But it is not as non-discriminatory as it seems. The choice of the particular articles which are prohibited was very carefully made in order to cause as little harm as possible to those countries from which we wish to get imports in order to help them in their dollar position. May I state to the house that during the twelve months ended June 30, 1947, the total imports of prohibited items from what we call the non-scheduled countries, that is, countries other than the United States and dollar countries, amounted to only $13,500,000. Of that total, at least $7,500,000 came from countries other than the United Kingdom, so that there would be only five or six million dollars worth of goods which would otherwise have come to this country. I make the statement that the restrictions which have been imposed will cause no real difficulty to the United Kingdom in exporting goods to this country. Under the quota system they will have an almost unlimited quota. I do not intend to go into details, but I did want to deal with that point which was raised by the leader of the C.C.F. group.
There is another point which he raised and with which I should like to deal. He said that prices were going up faster than wages and I should like to give some figures in connection with that. The cost of living index stands at 143.6. I should like to give the figures provided by the dominion bureau of statistics for average weekly earnings. I shall give the October 1 figure as compared with the average for 1939, which was 100.1. The figures I am giving can therefore be compared directly with the cost of living index, which was 100 in 1939. The figures are as follows:
Average
weekly
earnings
Manufacturing industry	 163-6
Logging industries	 223-3
Coal	 157-6
Mining	 151-5
Metals	 148-9
Communications	 139-2
That is the only one so far below the index figure. The other figures are:
Transport	 150-1
Street railways	 146-3
Construction and maintenance	 163-5
Services, hotels, restaurants, etc...	161-0
Trade	 137-2
Finance	 129-6
Finance is the lowest of the lot, a splendid example.
The Address-Mr. Abbott
Can the minister give the figures in dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Those are the average
weekly earnings as compared with the cost of living.
Those are percentages. Can the minister give the percentages in dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not those figures but they are readily available. I am comparing like with like. The suggestion made was that prices had risen faster than wages. Whatever the wage level may have been in 1939, my point is this, that wages have risen just as rapidly and in many cases much more rapidly than prices.
I should have said that they have not risen sufficiently to meet the increased cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I do want to refer to the Jeremiah charge which was made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition yesterday. He said, at page 48 of Hansard:
In about fifteen minutes after the Prime Minister had finished, the new Jeremiah came on the air.
He was referring to myself. He went on:
I am not an authority on Biblical affairs-
He might have extended the scope of that statement.
-but I understand that Jeremiah was the man who wrote the Book of (Lamentations. He was a prophet of gloom who prophesied, among other things, the coming of Nebuchadnezzar, the King.
The modern Jeremiah-
That is myself.
The modern Jeremiah went on the air and said, "We have been telling you that Canada was in splendid shape, but we are finding now that that was all a mistake, that as a matter of fact she is in pretty bad shape. I am appointed to tell you what the decrees are that we have prepared behind closed doors to fix everything up."
I did not say any such thing and I did not convey that impression of the Prime Minister's address to which my hon. friend referred.
Oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right. With the indulgence of the house, I will quote exactly what I said in the concluding paragraph of my radio address. I said this:
The truth is that we in Canada have been living somewhat beyond our means during the last year or more-not beyond what we could afford if the rest of the world was restored to economic health, but beyond what we can afford

in the world as it is today. We cannot expect to be completely prosperous when much of the rest of the world in which we live and on which we depend for a large part of our trade is just beginning to recover from the terrible destruction and dislocation of the war.
So we have to make adjustments to bring our national living standard within the limits of what we can afford in the difficult conditions that surround us. For most of us, this moderate measure of austerity-
May I interject to say that was the only reference I made to austerity, and I am sorry I used the word at all because it has been picked up and the government's program referred to as its austerity program, when no such impression was intended to be conveyed. I went on to say:
For most of us, this moderate measure of austerity will mean inconvenience and for some it will create difficulty. But a problem of this magnitude cannot be solved painlessly.
At the same time, let us keep our difficulties in their right perspective. In comparison with most of the rest of the world we are a very fortunate people. Our trouble arises from the misfortunes of other countries, not from any basic weakness in our own economy. Our basic position is sound. Our level of employment is at the maximum. We have a great and expanding capacity to produce. We are producing at a high level and at a relatively low cost. This country of ours has had a notable record of achievement during and after the war-a record which has given us a self-confidence and raised Canada's stature in the eyes of the world. Let us keep up that record in surmounting the present emergency, conscious of our responsibilities and confident of our great future.
Mr. Speaker, if that is the speech of a Jeremiah my knowledge of the Scriptures is less than that of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. No, Mr. Speaker. We are living, of course, in difficult times and have difficult problems, but I was struck by a statement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made in reply to a press man in Montreal the other day, as reported in a Montreal newspaper. The press man asked the Prime Minister if this was going to be a difficult session and the Prime Minister replied, "One of the joys of public life is trying to overcome difficult problems." May I add that the record of the Liberal party in solving difficult problems under the distinguished leadership of the right hon. gentleman who sits before me has been a very successful one, and I think, Mr. Speaker, that the government has the confidence of the people of this country to continue doing so.
I now move the adjournment of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, we are opposed to the adjournment of this debate, and were it not for the fact that it is now six o'clock and a recorded vote would take

Tariffs and Trade
considerable time we would call for a division on the motion. But we are prepared to let it go through now, on division, on the understanding that we are definitely opposed to being cut off at this time from our constitutional right to speak in this debate.
Motion agreed to on division, and debate adjourned.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
