subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the house will return to government notices of motions so that we may take the second motion that appears under my name on page three.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Mackenzie King
moves, seconded by Mr. St. Laurent:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve the general agreement on tariffs and trade, including the protocol of provisional application thereof, annexed to the final act of the
second session of the preparatory committee of the united nations conference on trade and employment held at Geneva from April 10 'to October 30, 1947, together with the complementary agreements of October 30, 1947, between Canada and the United States of America and between Canada and the United Kingdom; and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin to discuss the Geneva trade agreement, I might say a further word with reference to the question that has been raised by some lion, members as to why parliament was not called at an earlier day, having regard to the foreign exchange measures that have to come before it. That question has been answered in large part already, but I should like to leave, as part of the record, something in more exact terms.
The government has been giving serious attention to our foreign exchange problem for some time. However, that problem is basically a trade problem. Its long-term solution depends upon the development of multilateral world trade on a large scale. The government accordingly felt that it would be most unwise for any action to be taken with regard to our immediate problem without knowing, in a broad sense, what the longterm picture would be. That picture could not be known until the Geneva conference had concluded, since its decisions will have a more far-reaching influence on future trade than any other factors we may devise. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said on November 17 last, "the government felt it would be unwise to reach a final decision in regard to its program until it knew the results of the difficult and far-reaching trade negotiations which were being carried on at Geneva and until the prospects for implementation of the Marshall plan became more definite." Once these conditions became known, the government was able to complete its plans for rectification of our present exchange difficulties. Further time has, of course, been needed to get these emergency measures in final form for presentation to the house. The task has been a very large one, and the time that has been available has been less than would have been desirable. I think, from this, it will be clear that the session has been called at as early a day as it was felt it could effectively be called. I might add that, apart from the necessity of having some time after November 17 to put measures in final form, there has been an added advantage in that, since November 17, the country has had time to study the decisions that have been taken and to gain some clearer understanding of what is involved. This will be
Tariffs and Trade

of substantial assistance in the effective consideration of the legislative measures that will be presented.
As hon. members will recall, I took advantage at the outset of the session and before the introduction of any of these measures to indicate the program -and proposed procedure for the entire period between its opening and the adjournment for the Christmas of New Year recess. It might be helpful if, in a similar way, I were to indicate at once the procedure that it is suggested might be followed in the consideration of the Geneva agreement.
Broadly, there are three stages. First, there is the stage we have already entered upon, a consideration of the resolution for the approval of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. This resolution will afford an opportunity for the discussion of general principles; it will also serve -as an approach to the consideration of the large problem which the approval of the agreement itself involves.
The next stage proposed is a resolution seeking approval for the tariff provisions set forth in the schedules of the agreement. This resolution will be referred to the committee of ways and means where there will be opportunity for examination in detail of the provisions.
Finally, there will be the introduction of :he necessary legislation to give effect to the general agreement.
This procedure is the same as that which was followed in 1936 and again in 1939 in giving approval to the trade agreements between Canada and the United States. It will not be possible before Christmas to conclude these three stages, but consideration of the resolution now before the house will help to give to hon. members a pretty complete picture of the agreement, and of what will be involved or may be advisable in further discussions.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister state again what the second stage is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The second stage is a resolution to approve the tariff provisions. That resolution will be referred ;o the committee of ways and means where the various tariff provisions that are set forth in the schedule to the agreement will be considered in detail.
I might now say a word as to the origin of the Geneva agreement. It is some little time since the subject was first brought up in this house. It might revive the memories of hon. members were I to quote what I said when I first* made an announcement to the house concerning the proposed agreement.

The Geneva agreement had its origin in proposals by the United States government in December, 1945. In tabling the proposals in the house on December 12, 1945, I said:
The government of the United States has proposed that all countries should concert their efforts in the sphere of their international economic relations, with a view to expanding the volume of world trade and maintaining high and stable levels of national employment. The specific suggestions for achieving these ends, set forth in the document which is now being tabled for the consideration of members of parliament, deserve our most careful study, for no country has a greater interest than Canada in the realization of these objectives.
At all stages since, this government has maintained close and constant interest in this vital problem. At Geneva, Canada played a very important part, indeed a part of major importance, in the consideration of the agreement itself. The result of our efforts, in conjunction with those of other countries, is a crowning achievement, giving new hope and encouragement for the future.
Hon. members have, I believe, received copies of the final act of the Geneva conference and also copies of the press release of November 17 and of the schedule to the agreement. There -may be some who have not received copies of the press release, it will be available to any who have not thus far seen them. May I add a further word as to the background of the agreement. I have sought to bring this statement into as concise form as possible that it may serve as a ready reference to hon. members in considering the matter.
In December, 1945, at the signing of the financial agreement between the United States and the United Kingdom, proposals were set forth for "an expansion of world trade and employment." In February, 1946, the economic and social council of the united nations adopted a United States resolution constituting the preparatory committee of the international conference on trade and employment. On May 31,	1946, arrangements were
announced by the economic and social council for the preparatory committee to meet in London in October. From October 15 to November 26, 1946 the first session of the preparatory committee was held in London. Eighteen states had been named to the committee : Australia, Belgium, Luxemburg, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, France, India, Lebanon, The Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, the Union of South Africa, the United States, the United Kingdom and the U.S.S.R. The UJ3.S.R., however, did not attend.

Tariffs and Trade
From April 10 to October 30, 1947, the second session of the preparatory committee was held at Geneva. Twenty-three governments were represented, and the negotiations resulted in the conclusion of the general agreement on tariffs and trade now before the house. Further developments are at the present time under discussion at the conference that is being held in Havana. The agreements may be modified somewhat as a result of the Havana conference, but the government has thought it advisable to have the agreement approved as it is; and if modifications should be made at Havana, these modifications can be brought before the house, at a subsequent time, and the agreement itself amended as may be necessary.
I wish again to point out that, from the nature of the agreement and of the extensive tariff revisions which are included in the schedules, it is obvious that consideration cannot be completed for some time and by no chance before the Christmas adjournment. This will not affect the protocol by which Canada has agreed to bring parts I and II of the agreement along with the tariff provisions in schedule V into effect provisionally on January 1, 1948.
Schedule V can be brought into effect by action of the governor in council under section 11 of the Customs Tariff Act. Part II of the agreement will come into effect only in so far as it is not inconsistent with existing legislation. The countries with which the agreement will come into effect on January 1 are Australia. Belgium. Canada. France. Luxembourg, The Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States.
I wish now to say a word in regard to the character of the general agreement. The general agreement on tariffs and trade is what its name implies, a document of a comprehensive nature which embodies the widest measure of agreement on trading practices and for tariff reductions that the nations of the world have ever witnessed. It represents the culmination of several months of negotiations on questions of tariffs and trading practices at Geneva. It is an accomplishment of the most far-reaching importance for this country and for the world. Together, the agreement and the charter of the proposed international trade organization represent a balanced and inclusive effort to promote world peace by prosperity and economic co-operation. For Canada the importance of the general agreement can scarcely be exaggerated. The freeing of world trade on a broad multilateral basis is of fundamental importance for our entire national welfare. Let me- say a further word on the importance of international trade for Canada. On February 14. 1939, in moving the 5849-74
resolution for approval of the trade agreement of November 17, 1938, between Canada and the United States, I spoke as follows with regard to the importance of international trade for Canada:
A policy of national self-sufficiency is out of the question for Canada, which is peculiarly in need of international trade because of its enormous production of primary commodities and its relatively small population. Thus we cannot, like some other countries, pursue a policy of producing all that we consume and consuming all that we produce. Our whole economy, the prosperity of our vast wheat areas, our mines and forests and fisheries, and our far-flung transportation systems, are based upon the continuance of international exchange of goods on a great and growing scale. The restriction of international exchanges involves a declining standard of living, as -the totalitarian nations have found to their cost. The increase of international exchange of goods involves a rising standard of living, not for ourselves alone, but for all peoples that are ready to join with us in removing -the obstacles which at present obstruct the free course of international trade.
Canada, then, on both political and economic grounds, is committed to a policy of peace and good will, and of freer exchange with countries which will meet us half way.
May I now say a word about the developments since 1939. They have not altered the basic situation. The industrial productivity of Canada is much greater. There is a somewhat increased diversification of the industrial base, but the fundamental position of Canada in relation to trading is unchanged. We still have vast production and small population; we still have emphasis on an enormous output of a relatively small number of commodities. We still rely mainly on production and processing of primary products. We cannot for one moment contemplate the possibility of becoming self-sufficient and consuming all we produce, or of producing all we consume. The level of external trade is the fundamental determinant of the prosperity of Canada, of our level of employment and of our standard of living.
A word next as to the importance of multilateral trade. Fundamentally we are concerned not only over the level of our own external trade, but we have also a fundamental concern for the level of external trade of other countries. The character of our trade, with surpluses of exports to certain countries, and excesses of imports from other countries, requires a condition in which surpluses on one account can be converted to offset deficiencies on another account. This means that a bilateral approach to trade is not enough. We cannot prosper on the basis simply of reciprocal agreements with single countries. Perhaps more than any other country we stand to
Tariffs and Trade

prosper from the prosperity of others. We are interested in the welfare not only of our customers, but of our customers' customers. A high level of multilateral trade on the broadest possible basis is what we seek. The Geneva agreement is the most important and most hopeful development toward this goal that has yet been achieved.
. I should like to say that it is a source of particular gratification to me that the present agreement should be so completely in line with what has been the policy of the Liberal party in Canada from the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier down to the present time, and that it should be my privilege to present it to our parliament. The Liberal party has always been in the van in the struggle for greater freedom of trade. Throughout its history, it has always believed that without multilateral trade on a broad basis Canada can never be really prosperous. We have always seen the implications of our economy based upon abundant but highly specialized resources. The party has always acted on the belief that prosperity is inevitably associated with extensive and general international commerce. There has been full recognition of this important fact by the Liberals in government, in parliament and in the country as a whole.
Here I should like to draw attention to the significance of preferences as they have been viewed by the Liberal party since they were first introduced in 1896. Tariffs, when applied by Liberal regimes, except in very special cases and in difficult, disturbing periods, have been for revenue purposes, with protection only incidental. Preferences, when applied by Liberal governments, have had the basic purpose of stimulating trade through the reduction of duties rather than by increasing them. The whole Liberal policy with respect to tariffs and preferences has been formed with a view to increasing world commerce and enlarging opportunities of trade.
The so-called imperial preference policy was inaugurated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It was associated with a general lowering of tariffs, and under the administration of Sir Wilfrid there was a general lowering of tariffs, with the reductions made gradually to avoid any disruption of industry, together with an attempt to achieve reciprocity with the United States. Before the Liberal administration under Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power, there had been a period of depression and stagnation. The country grew prosperous under the stimulus of ever-increasing trade.
Again from 1921 to 1930, during the first years of the present administration, there were reductions in the duties on many imported

articles. As it was in the 1890's so it was at the beginning of the 1920's. The country was in the throes of a depression. Changes in tariffs were made with the view of helping the country by reducing costs of production in agriculture, mining, forestry, fishing and other industries. The rates on articles of general consumption were reduced, and, with expanding external trade made possible by reductions in tariffs, our country reached the most prosperous era in its history up to that time.
This may not be so pleasant for my hon. friends of the official opposition; nevertheless it is true that when the Conservative party came into office in 1930 there developed again a period of depression. We cannot blame any one person or any one group for this world condition.

speechtext:
Thank you. Mr. Speaker. I did not expect that my hon. friends of the official opposition would like this, but I hope that for a little while they will be able to take it.
As I have said, the agreements of 1935 and 1938 with the United States were of outstanding significance. As far as the producers of this country were concerned, there -were great benefits secured on a wide variety of goods. Consumers likewise were greatly benefited.
The duties chargeable under the British preference were progressively reduced. They reached the point where the average rates were lower than they had been at any other time.
The entire history of the Liberal party on tariff and trade matters has emphasized a policy of reducing restrictions, of lowering tariffs and stimulating Canadian prosperity by stimulating the trade of the world.
One aspect of Liberal policy I wish to make clear is that the basis on which the Liberals have acted for fifty years in the matter of giving preferences has been by lowering tariffs and reducing restrictions, or through the British preference. Imperial preferences originated in a resolution in this parliament in 1897, as I have said, under the regime of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The preference, as it relates to the customs tariff, is a means whereby the country to which the preference is accorded is given the right to have its commodities enter a country at a rate of duty less than that imposed against countries generally. LTnder the British preference in 1897, it was provided that goods coming into Canada from Britain should enter this country at 12i per cent less than the generally prevailing rate. By 1900 the preference had been increased to 33-j per cent. In 1907 the British preferences were completely overhauled; entirely new schedules of rates were established with individual margins substantially below most favoured nation rates.
The nature of the preference, as originally conceived and applied under the Laurier administration, was that preferences were granted, let me repeat, through reduction of duties on British goods, not through increases in the tariffs on the goods of other countries. The original basis and approach of the British preference continued until 1932. Changes in preferences were effected by reduction in duties or by placing commodities on the free list. The Liberal approach to the British preference as well as the Liberal approach to tariffs in general were set forth by me in an address to the house on May 23. 1923. It constantly emphasized the importance of looking toward reductions in duties. Referring to the further features of the budget for 1923, I stated:
' In the first place, there are in it. so far as tariff matters are concerned, a very large number of reductions in duties. I have in my hand a list of tariff reductions in which some 21 different items have been affected by considerable reductions, apart altogether from the general reduction made through the British preference on all articles. Twenty-one different articles, which I will not detain the house by reading, have been affected by an immediate reduction of duty. Then, as respects all com-
Tariffs and Trade

modifies, the British preference has been increased. This is equivalent to a reduction in the customs duty on articles coming from Great Britain of a 10 per cent discount on all goods coming in through our Canadian ports. There again is a further general reduction of duties. But let me point out to hon. gentlemen that this budget must be considered not only in relation to what we are doing at the moment but in conjunction with what we did last year. Last year we made some material reductions in customs duties, some of them with respect to the British preference; and if one takes occasion to study carefully the items that were affected, one will find that as regards goods coming from the old country there has been a very considerable reduction in customs duties through an increase of the British preference. I have here a list of items that have been affected by the British preference in a very direct way and to a considerable degree by what we have done this session combined with what was done last year. In some 40 cases which I might cite there have been reductions ranging anywhere from 2 to 3, 4, 5, 7 and 9 per cent increase in the British preference.
In addition to regarding the British preference as a process of tariff reduction, Liberal governments have also regarded preferences as purely a voluntary undertaking, not as something contractual.
I think it is important that hon. members should see the difference in the point of view of hon. gentlemen on this side and some on the other as to a consideration we regard as all-important in the matter of granting preferences. We have never, at any time, intended that preferences should prejudice, in any way, our trading with countries other than those within the British commonwealth of nations. We have always intended that the preference should give us all the advantage which might be gained by trading with nations of the British commonwealth, but at the same time that it should not deprive us of every opportunity of freely entering into agreements with other countries.
Our preferences were entered into in a broad spirit of willingness to become, in ever-increasing measure, good customers to those who treat us in a like manner. The method is one of voluntary concessions arrived at after negotiations aiming to discover what is of mutual interest and mutual benefit, and not through hard bargaining.
The governing principles in granting preferences have been mutual benefits to the countries concerned; the stimulation of competition by keeping costs down; the reduction of eosts for exporting industries, enabling them to enter foreign markets more successfully, and generally the promotion of increased trade.
With the preferences of 1932, the whole princip'e was changed by the so-called Ottawa

trade agreements. The general schedules of tariff rates, were by those agreements substantially increased. Even the British preferential rates were raised in many cases against commonwealth products. The preference was accorded through raising duties against all other nations to unprecedented heights. Within this framework, the countries of the British commonwealth granted certain preferences to each other.
In 1932 Canada and the other countries in the commonwealth adopted a protectionist policy. Under the 1932 agreements, the result of the new form of preferences was a decrease in the total trade, rather than an increase.
After 1935, and up to the beginning of the war, various trade agreements resulted in a major reconstruction of the Canadian tariff. Under the British preferential tariff the rates of duty chargeable against the United Kingdom were once more adjusted in a downward direction. There was a renewed effort to free the channels of trade by returning the preference to a basis of tariff reduction rather than a basis of tariff increase.
Now, in regard to the part played by preferences at the Geneva conference, I would say that margins of preference, as well as rates of duty, played an important part in those negotiations. The general approach was in favour of equality of treatment and of general tariff reduction, through a diminution of margins of preference.
The basic principles of agreement at Geneva on preferences were:	No new preferences
were to be created; no existing preferences were to be enlarged; preferences remaining in effect w'ere to be negotiable; that is to say, they were to be capable of being reduced or narrowed by negotiating with foreign countries in return for concessions to one, or other (or both) of the preference parties.
Canada wras involved in two directions in the negotiations with respect to preferences at Geneva. First, there were demands by foreign countries for reductions of preferences enjoyed by Canada in other parts of the commomvealth and, second, there were demands for reductions of preferences granted by Canada to other countries of the commonwealth.
Canada followed at Geneva the basic principle adopted in the origins of the preference under Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We strongly opposed any narrowing of preferential margins by the device of raising preferential tariff rates. In all the provisions in schedule V there is only one instance of raising a duty under the British preferential tariff. In all other cases, where the preference is narrowed, a reduction was achieved by reducing the tariff rate applicable to non-British countries.

Tariffs and Trade
Canada was prepared to see the same principle applied with regard to preference for her products in other countries of the commonwealth. Canada agreed in several cases to the reduction of preferential margins previously enjoyed.
In addition to reduction in duties applicable to non-British countries and to reduction in preference margins, there were a large number of cases of absolute reductions in duties against British goods.
The policy of tariff reduction runs through the entire agreement. While the basis of the British preference has been altered by agreement, which restricts the preference to items set forth in the schedules, these have been drafted so broadly that neither Canada nor any other commonwealth country has given up any preferential position which it regarded as important. The schedules were most carefully scrutinized and worked out in minute detail. Schedule -XIX establishes the preference position for all items in which Canada is seriously interested in the United Kingdom market. Schedule V does the same for all items in which the United Kingdom is seriously interested in the Canadian market. The same applies, on a reciprocal basis, in these and other schedules with regard to other parts of the commonwealth.
At this point I should like to make reference to the exchange of notes with the United Kingdom under date of October 30, 1947, which establishes the present position with respect to preferences between our country and the United Kingdom.
The United Kingdom and Canada mutually recognize the right of each to reduce or eliminate preferences remaining after the conclusion of the general agreement. But favourable tariff treatment is assured by agreement against raising rates against the others' products in schedules V and XIX of the general agreement above the level in force before the war. The effect of the exchange of notes is to give freedom of negotiation and to make it possible to return to the original basis of preference.
I made a statement from London on this matter, and perhaps I might be permitted to repeat it at this time. My statement was made on the evening of November 17. At that time I said:
In initiating preferences fifty years ago, the Canadian government of that day had in mind the voluntary granting of tariff preferences to one another by the different parts of the British commonwealth of nations. It was not intended that there should grow up a system which would prejudice the maintenance of friendly relations with other countries. On the contrary what was envisaged was a system whereby trade would be
increased among British countries, full opportunity being afforded at the same time for -the expansion of their trade with other countries.
If Canada is to play its part in furthering the objectives of the international trade organization, it is important that the Canadian government should have freedom to determine the extent to which it shall maintain preferential arrangements while carrying out its obligations under the charter. We do not consider that a system under which -the power to reduce the Canadian tariff may be dependent upon the consent of other governments is consistent either with the spirit in which preferences were originally extended by the Canadian government, or with -those principles upon which continuing cooperation in economic matters can be carried on between the countries of the British commonwealth.
In order to assure the success of this agreement, the fundamental aim of the government now and in the future will be to work toward the successful operation of the agreement. The temporary problem of the present in the form of a United States dollar shortage has necessitated interim emergency measures which appear to be in conflict with the fundamentals of the agreement, but it must be kept constantly in mind that they are temporary, that they are of an emergency character and that they are subordinate in aim and purpose to the general agreement. .
The government would not previously, and will not at any time, allow them to imperil the success of the general agreement. It would have been the height of folly during the Geneva discussions to have allowed premature announcement of emergency measures to have confused or endangered the negotiations. In matters of this kind, there is nothing more important than timing. Temporary measures are needed to bring about the basic adjustment that will enable us to go forward under the Geneva program.
As I said in London on November 17:
At all times and at all costs we must keep our real and long-run objectives constantly in sight. We must meet the requirements of the short-run situation courageously, competently and with confidence, accepting emergency measures for what they are-drastic but temporary adjustments. By making sure that the emergency measures we have to take are not permitted to hamper or distort our long-run objectives, we shall, by the enlarged opportunities for world trade made public today, be greatly furthering our country's growth and development. It is to wider horizons that Canada must ever look.
Under the general agreement, it is indeed to wide horizons that Canada is looking. We look to a future in which the productive capacity of nations will be restored; in which trade of all countries will be enabled to flow freely; in which economic and commercial co-operation will form the basis for political
Tariffs and Trade

harmony; and in which the interests of humanity will be served by the mutual prosperity of all nations.

One can imagine that the Prime Minister has put forward the best side of the case to be made for this trade agreement. I want to be perfectly neutral in my approach to this question and deal with it on its merits rather than as a political issue. However, as the Prime Minister has put forward the best side of it, I think I should point out something on the other side.
I would have been more impressed with what the Prime Minister has just said if the so-called short-term program of the government had not completely nullified many of the good things hoped for from the agreements. For example, what good does it do to increase the number of cattle that are to be allowed to be shipped from Canada to the United States from 225,000 to 400,000 a year if we are to have an embargo which says that we cannot ship any at all? What good does it do to have the tariff on wheat reduced from forty-two cents to twenty-two cents a bushel when the United States has some hundreds of millions of bushels of wheat each year more than She needs?
One would have been more impressed if there had not been so much of these embargoes against goods coming into this country. Embargoes are not low-tariff proposals; they are the highest form of protection. One would have been more impressed if there had not been this rationing by the government. One would have been more impressed if there had not been restrictive provisions such as the government has brought in. One would have been more impressed if what the government is doing now was not resulting in higher prices to everybody with the threat of considerable unemployment immediately before us.
Let us all admit that this kind of arrangement is important. I think everyone from one side of this nation to the other recognizes that. But I want to say at the moment that it was not necessary to consider

these agreements at this particular time. They offer little help for the immediate problem which is facing the country. What help they do offer could have been achieved without any talk here at all, in which case we might have been allowed to proceed to deal with what the government really brought us here to deal with, the objectionable restrictive measures which it has brought in.
The government did not need to bring us here to discuss these agreements. Measures of this kind have been dealt with in the past, and last night I referred to one in 1935 and another in 1938. At that time agreements were made in the fall of the year at about the same time as these were made. These agreements were put into effect provisionally on January 1 by order in council under the provisions of the customs act. Nothing was done in the way of legislation until four months after the agreements were made. That procedure could have been followed on this occasion. We would have had the advantage of whatever merit they have, and I admit that they have merit, without having to take up time now in talking about them.
I need not repeat what I said last night. I hold in my hand a copy of the trade agreement of 1938. As I said, it was entered into on November 17, 1938, and brought into force by order in council under legislation already on the statute books. That agreement came into effect provisionally on January 1. I need not go through all the steps, but parliament did not meet until a couple of months later. The measure then went through all stages; and four months after the agreement was made, it was approved by legislation. That procedure could have been followed instead of taking up time now to discuss these matters. 1 suggest that these agreements were brought before us now just as window-dressing for the objectionable measures which we shall be proceeding with later on.
I wish to refer to two or three of the points the Prime Minister made. He offered the government's excuse as to why parliament had not been called at an earlier day, or why its own steps to meet this crisis had not been taken earlier. He said the government considered it was unwise to do so until the Geneva conference had been concluded. I have just two observations to make on that. The first is that several other countries interested in the expansion of trade did not see things that way. They went ahead, weeks before the Geneva conference was concluded, and took steps to meet their own problems. Britain was one of those countries; France was another; Australia -was another; Ceylon was another, and there were others as well.

Tariffs and Trade
My other observation on the excuse which the Prime Minister gives for delay is that, while the government was waiting, this crisis was developing and getting worse at the rate of about 880,000,000 a month. The situation is all the more serious now because the government dealt with it late and because it called parliament into session late. I do not need to point out again that whatever measures the government has taken are or could have been put into effect without our being here at all just now.
The Prime Minister then referred to the question of procedure. He pointed out that on the order paper there are two resolutions, one dealing with the general agreement on tariffs and trade and a second one to which I shall refer a little later. I wish to say now that I do not like the procedure which the government has planned and I do not think the house will. What it means is this. We shall be asked to pass this first resolution without the opportunity of having it go to a committee where the government and the government's experts could be examined upon it. It is now planned to have the second resolution go to the committee of the whole house unless other arrangements are made. We think provision should be made to have the first resolution go to a committee where we could ask questions and seek explanations and information upon it.
Then the Prime Minister, not unexpectantly, referred to the conditions that existed between the years 1930 and 1935. One can imagine what his purpose was in referring to conditions at that time. After the Prime Minister had finished telling us what a wonderful low-tariff government his government had been, it was surprising to me to be told that, after having been here for about a quarter of a century, his government should have brought us into the serious condition we are facing today.
What is the condition we are facing today? It is a condition of unfavourable trade balances for Canada as against the United States, amounting to nearly $1,000 million a year. But since the Prime Minister has referred to the years from 1930 to 1935, let me refer to the five years prior to 1930 and to all the years after 1945 in connection with this question of our unfavourable trade balance with the United States which the government now admits is a crisis. Our unfavourable trade balance means that we are buying more from the United States than we are selling to them and that we have not the money to pay for the adverse balance.
What were our unfavourable trade balances with the United States in the years from 1925 H849-8
to 1930? I have the figures here, taken from official government reports. I shall give them in round figures.
In 1925 we had an unfavourable trade balance with the United States of $92,000,000; 1926, $210,000,000; 1927, $239,000,000; 1928, $344,000,000; and 1929, $400,000,000.
That is the way in which this government solved the problem of an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States in the years from 1925 to 1930, and that is why we have the problem with which we are faced today.
Now let us take the years after 1935 on. In 1936 we had an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States of $35,000,000.

The Prime Minister mentioned one other thing, what he called the exchange of notes between Canada and Great Britain by w'hich each country reserves the right to reduce or eliminate the British preferences without consulting the other. I wish to observe that that exchange of notes has nothing whatever to do with the general trade agreement we are here to consider. True, it is a part of the government's program but it is a thing apart altogether from the general trade agreement.
Tariffs and, Trade

I wish now to read the resolution with which we are dealing. It is moved by the Prime Minister:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve the general agreement on tariffs and trade, including the protocol of provisional application thereof, annexed to the final act of the second session of the preparatory committee of the united nations conference on trade and employment held at Geneva from April 10 to October 30, 1947, together with the complementary agreements of October 30, 1947, between Canada and the United States of America and between Canada and the United Kingdom-
So in this resolution we are asked to approve the general agreement and also the exchange of notes that passed between Canada and the United Kingdom. The resolution goes on:
-and that this house do approve of the same, subject -to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.
So the resolution with which we are dealing seeks the approval of the house not only for the general agreement but for the exchange of notes which passed between this government and the British government and which have the effect I maintain, of washing out the British preferences altogether. One might ask now, why that procedure? I suggest that we should separate these two parts and deal with the general agreements by themselves and the other agreement-the exchange of letters-by itself.
As to the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party with respect to trade matters generally, let me say this. We favour the widest possible measure of international trade consistent with preserving our own standard of living in Canada; and I might add that that statement carries out the spirit of our platform approved at Winnipeg in December, 1942, which reads:
We endorse the aims expressed in the Atlantic charter and believe that Canada should join in the setting up of effective international measures to give them practical application, correcting trade barriers, with a view to making the world's resources available without discrimination for the satisfaction of human needs.
That statement of policy, as hon. members will have noticed, referred to the Atlantic charter. I might read the clause in the Atlantic charter to which it applies. It is the fourth paragraph of that document and reads: Fourth, they will endeavour with due respect for their existing obligations, to further the enjoyment by all states, great or small, victor or vanquished, of access on equal terms to the trade and to the raw materials of the world which are needed for their economic prosperity.
That is the statement with respect to trade which appears in the Atlantic charter. One 
might pause for a moment to refer to one section of that statement, to be found in the first line:
They will endeavour, with due respect for their existing obligations-
That is a clause which we understand was incorporated in that statement because those who were representing the British government at that time did not want to see the British preference wiped out by that charter.
What the government should do now in connection with the British preferences incorporated in this resolution is this:	First, it
should take out the special agreement with Britain and deal with each part by itself. The agreement with Britain has nothing to do with the Geneva trade agreements. I pointed that out before. Second, th'e government should put the Geneva trade agreements part of the first resolution, and the second resolution covering schedule 5, together in one resolution, and that should go to a committee, so that members, before finally accepting or rejecting it, can examine, not only the tariff concessions we make, but those general, sweeping clauses in the agreement by which we shall be bound.
I suggest that as a procedure because I believe that by that means the members of the house will get a better understanding of the advantages of the arrangements, the weaknesses of them, if there are any, and the full effect of them.
Just a word now about the British-Cana-dian agreement. In the Geneva trade agreements some of our preferences with Britain have been lost; for example, the preference on apples. That is important, particularly to Nova Scotia and to British Columbia. If these agreements are approved, there will be no preference left on apples. One might ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) to explain why that- preference was let go.
After the trade agreements are in effect, as of January 1, we shall have lessened the British preferences, but some preferences will still be left, namely on lumber, which is important to British Columbia. But the exchange of letters with Britain paves the way for the end of this preference and of others. These letters between the two governments pave the way for the end of anything that is left now of British preference. One might read sections 2 and 6 of the Canadian letter dated October 30, and that will be made clear. Other preferences left after the general agreement is passed concern motor cars, newsprint and a vast area of colonial preferences, but they are all in danger under this exchange of letters.

Tariffs and Trade
As I have said, these letters-these notes so-called-mean the death knell of the British preference system.
The principle of this agreement seems to be the most-favoured-nation principle. What it means is that we cannot favour our customers or anyone else, and neither our customers nor anyone else can favour us by way of trade concessions and so on. In the ease of the United States, where we have a huge unfavourable trade balance, we cannot take long-term special measures to correct the situation by tariff and trade agreements unless what we do applies to every other country .in the agreement.
That has been the situation to a degree for some eleven years. In 1935 some such agreement was made with the United States. That was the first time Canada granted the United States the same treatment as all other foreign countries. But now, under these Geneva trade agreements, we go farther and give the United States the same treatment as all others, including British commonwealth countries, in any future arrangements we may make.' Under the exchange of letters we lay the basis for shutting out the balance of British preferences for good.
Schedule 5 contains the concessions we make. I suggest that we should examine the concessions we are required to make with a view to seeing what we get for them. That is the real problem which is facing us in this kind of agreement. Do we get as much as we give? For example, we had valuable advantages that are now lost. One is in regard to apples. What do wTe gain in return for giving up the advantage we had? We want to see what we get in return for what we give up.
We know that any arrangement of this kind must be regarded as a two-way' street. We must not expect other folks to give up everything and ourselves to give up nothing. But it is well, in an agreement of this kind, to see what we are giving up and what we are getting in return. What I suggest now is that the house will want to know what the deal is. I need only point out that we have lost whatever advantage we had, not only on apples, but on frozen salmon, canned pears, vegetables, honey, electric stoves, typewriters, and half of the lumber preference, and many other items.
May I say a word further with respect to the procedure proposed by the government? I mentioned it in my opening remarks because the Prime Minister had referred to it. I say the procedure as we now have it outlined is confusing. We are asked to pass one resolution here without ever having an opportunity 5849-8J
to examine anybody' about it. The passage of that resolution means that the other one is passed at the same time, because the first one includes the substance of the second. The second one approves the concessions in the agreement and asks for a bill to approve it. As I said, the first resolution includes the second. If we approve the first we shall have approved the second. But it means that the first one will not go to a committee; that the second one will go to a committee of whatever kind the government determines, perhaps just a committee of the whole, but I hope it will be more than that. It means that if we approve the first we swallow all before we have had a chance to examine the agreements in detail or to question the government or to question the experts. I suggest that that is not a generous way to treat hon. members with respect to this measure. I think everybody in the house wants to find that he can support this measure. I have not seen any evidence that anybody wants to make it a partisan issue. I suggest that the first resolution should go to a committee before we are asked to vote upon it.
We in this party have had a small committee trying to study these agreements. I think it is true to say that never was parliament called upon to pass upon such a mass of interlacing and complicated ideas. Personally I want to be optimistic about them. I do not want to throw cold water on these plans, but in a field so complicated there is a wide scope for honest and different opinions. I merely suggest to the government that they give us an opportunity to have more light shed upon the pros and cons of this whole thing before we vote upon the resolution before us.
The spirit of the agreement seems to be that we tie ourselves against doing something which is regarded as bad in the family of nations; and then we find escape clauses which will let us do that which we agreed not to do. In our study of these measures we have seen several contradictions. We read one clause which appears to tie our hands, and then we find an escape clause by which our hands are untied. We seem to be tied in some measure at least against domestic subsidies to Alberta and Nova Scotia coal, but then we find what looks like an out clause by which we are not tied. We should like to know exactly what the position is with respect to the many situations of that kind.
We read in another place that the tariff concessions must not be frustrated or defeated by special advantages to domestic producers. There seem to be escape clauses here also. Let

Tariffs and Trade

the government tell us, let them bring their experts to help them tell us, whether the sum total of these provisions put together means something worth while to us or not.
May I say a word about articles XII, XIII and XIV? Article XII says that we can take special domestic measures to protect our .balance of payments. It is under this provision that the special powers bill and the excise amendments will be brought in. We can therefore deal with them when they come before us.
In article XIII we are asked to agree to treat all parties to the agreement equally. It means that we can make no preferential agreements with anyone. Article XIV seems to provide the possibilities of a complete escape as far as Britain is concerned, that we do not have to apply the government's stringent measures against British goods coming into this country; in other words we shall not have to apply the present quota and prohibition restrictions against Britain. In that connection I just wish to ask the government three questions, and I am sure they will be glad to answer them as they proceed to interpret these agreements. Am I right in saying that we do not have to apply these measures against Britain? Are we applying them against Britain? If we are, why are we doing so? If we do not have to do it and are doing it, why are we doing it? I mention this matter only to show that our minds are far from clear from what we read in this document, and we want to have them made clear.
May I say a word about the Excise Tax Act? The excise tax which the government is bringing in applies to domestic as well as to imported products. This would appear not to be necessary under the agreement. If so, why is the government applying the special excise tax against domestic-made refrigerators as well as imported refrigerators? The Financial Post says they are applying the tax domestically because of diplomatic pressure from Washington. I make no comment about that. But I think the government should make clear whether that is the reason or not. If that is not the reason, then they should tell us why they are imposing this tax on domestically produced goods.
I now wish to refer to another aspect of this agreement that has come to our attention. It has to do with the effect of it on railway labour in Canada. Article V of the Geneva agreement has the effect of granting to United States highway transportation the privilege of carrying United States goods in bond across Canada. In its essence this will mean the sacrifice of the jobs of many Cana-[Jlr. Bracken.]
dian railway employees for the sake of benefiting a few United States truckers.
For years United States trucking interests have been seeking the privilege of carrying freight across the Canadian border in bond In particular they have sought to use this privilege to permit them to carry freight in bond between Detroit and Buffalo. Canadian railway employees, knowing that this would mean the sacrifice of jobs for many of them, have consistently fought this move. Under pressure, the Canadian government admitted the thin edge of the wredge during the last three years of the war by allowing the movement of United States war material by trucks in bond across Canadian territory. The Department of National Revenue knows that this regulation was never adequately enforced and, in the nature of things, could not be. The bonding privilege of these United States truckers was terminated two years ago for good reasons.
Now, under pressure of these United States interests the Canadian government has permitted the United States representatives to smuggle into the trade agreement a provision which will open up our boundaries and our highways to United States traffic moving from United *States points of origin to United States points of destination, employing United States labour and using United States equipment. Canadian railway labour is rightly alarmed at this prospect, because it unquestionably will mean loss of jobs to many Canadian railway employees
Railway labour organizations and many municipal councils, boards of trade and chambers of commerce have already voiced their strong opposition to the government's proposal. It is the government's first duty in this instance to preserve the jobs of our Canadian railway men.
I wish now to speak more generally about the major question that is before us, namely, the trade agreement as distinguished from the exchange of letters with respect to the British preference.
A freely trading world has been the ideal goal which has inspired every government since the end of world war one. Our declaration upon this subject made at Winnipeg m 1942 is and will remain the basis of our policy in the matter of international trade. I need not read it again.
We have now before us for consideration these proposed trade agreements. It will be admitted that none of our institutiors, including these, is of itself miraculous. They are vital only when they work for all the people. All

Tariffs and Trade
the institutions we set up to facilitate world trade must be based upon the facts of Canada's economy. We want to know what those facts are. Some of them I propose to summarize this evening. They are important. And we ought to keep them in mind as we proceed.
Of our total foreign trade, eighty-five per cent at all times is carried on with two economic units, namely with the sterling area represented by the British commonwealth and empire on the one hand, and with the United States of America on the other. The sterling area takes an average of fifty per cent of all our exports. With this sterling area we have always had a favourable balance of trade, which has amounted to the huge sum of $14,000 million since confederation and to more than $5,900 million within the last twenty-two years. With this sterling area we always have a favourable balance of payments, which has amounted to more than $7,609 million in the last twenty-two year-:. Finally our exports to the British commonwealth have a high labour content; that is, many jobs are involved in their production. Some products do not provide much labour, but many of these exports to the sterling area do have a large labour content.
On the other hand, the United States is a market in which we buy heavily, but in which we do not sell nearly as much as we buy. Hence we have had an unbroken unfavourable balance of trade with the United States for sixty-seven years. That unfavourable balance amounts to over $9,800 million since confederation and to over $5,600 milljpn in the last twenty-two years. Our balance of payments also is unfavourable to the extent of just under $7,000 million in the last twenty-two years. Further, three-quarters of our exports to the United States have a relatively low labour content; in other words, relatively few jobs are involved in their production.
It should be noted that the rest of the British commonwealth has taken a steadily increasing proportion of our exports through those years; yet we have taken a steadily declining proportion of our imports from them. Our exports to them have been going up; our imports from them have been going down. Is it any wonder they are in a bad way? It should be noted also that exactly the reverse has taken place in our relations with the United States of America. The proportion of our exports to the United States has declined while the proportion of our imports from that country has risen. Even in pre-war years two-thirds of our total imports from all countries came from the United
States. It is still higher at the present time. Hence our unfavourable balance of payments on the average has steadily increased.
In the light of these essential facts concerning Canada's trade and economy, what do the Geneva trade agreements do? That is the important question we have to answer in analysing this problem. Let me indicate a number of things I think these agreements do.
From our examination it appears that the average takings of our exports by each of the signatories outside the British commonwealth and the United States is 1-3 per cent of our total exports. The average amount we import from each of these same countries is one-quarter of one per cent of our total imports. The treaties, therefore, do not appear to have much material significance for us outside of their effect upon our British and our United States trade.
Under the terms of the treaties we lose all freedom of action in directing the course of our trade. I think that is the principle of the proposals. In no circumstance can we make special arrangements to buy from those who buy from us unless we offer the same privileges to all others. In the British market we gain no advantages whatever; in fact we shall lose some, and they gain nothing from us which is not shared equally by others.
According to a New York Times estimate of our trade with the United States, they gain advantage in items which in '1939 amounted to $354,000,000, or seventy-one per cent of our total imports from the United States. Further, Canada was oalled upon to make by far the greatest single sacrifice to America, covering nearly thirty per cent of all the primary concessions made at Geneva which, according to the estimate of the New York Times, amounted to $1,192,346,000.
What has Canada gained in return? The items upon which effective concessions are obtained, that is concessions which might be expected to increase our trade, amounted to only $134,000,000 in 1939, thirty-three per cent of our total sales to the United States. In 1946 those items of export amounted to only $260,000,000, or. thirty per cent of our total exports. It is claimed in press dispatches from Washington that the United States tariff barriers have been lowered to the 1913 level; but I think it is fair to point out that even in 1913 our adverse balance of trade with the United States was $297,200,000. Is the United States getting back to the position of 1913? Even so, our adverse balance of trade in that year was very large.
Further, Mr. Speaker, some of the alleged concessions are totally ineffective. With the
Tariffs and Trade

increasing exhaustion of United States resources, Canada is rapidly becoming America's principal source of supply. Their purchases here represent their needs, and these reductions in tariff merely aid their domestic consumers, while they do not stimulate our exports. This applies to lumber and base metals in particular.
In addition to our other difficulties, we learn that the United States customs authorities will add the Canadian excise tax of twenty-five per cent to the value of this class of goods for customs purposes, which will operate to reduce substantially or even exclude some of the exports we are now sending to the United States. But we seem to be rendered powerless to help ourselves in our extremity. Article I. paragraph 1 of the final act forbids any measure designed to direct or divert trade in any manner, no matter how desirable or necessary it may be. We have completely lost all freedom of action.
The chief folly of the government is, in our judgment, the destruction of the imperial preference system by their letter of October 30 to the government of the United Kingdom. The treaties forbid any increase in existing preferences, and forbid any new preferences; but the government has gone beyond this and appears to have embarked upon a campaign of destruction, of our best and greatest market, the market which maintains the employment and income of thousands of Canadians everywhere. As we see it now, we are opposed to the agreement contained in the letters of exchange between this government and the United Kingdom. It is foreign to and quite outside the Geneva agreement, and gives the finish to the empire preference system. By these letters the government invites the end of that great preferential trade structure.
I wish now to refer in some detail to the pattern of our British and American trade, wholly for the purpose of understanding what it is. The vital questions for Canada are these: What are the basic facts in our British and our American trade? In what way will these Geneva agreements affect, and be affected by, these facts?
I have some statistics on this subject which, with the permission of the house, I should like to have placed on Hansard in tabular form.

Thus each dollar of British exports represents more employment in Canada than does each dollar of exports to America. I am pointing out these facts for one purpose, namely to emphasize the importance of a market that we are steadily losing. That is the point I wish to make. The facts are incontrovertible; they are more eloquent than words. But what did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) say in Montreal on October 30? He said: "The United States has been and will remain a market for our goods which exceeds all others." When he said that he did not state the facts. The facts of the matter, no matter on what basis the claim is made, are quite the reverse. Even the United Kingdom alone has been, in the past, a larger market than America.	.
With what does the government now confront us, and ask that we ratify? Our problem has been a chronic adverse trade balance with the United States. That is why the government entered into all these arrangements. That is why we are here in December,
rather than in January or February. What do these agreements do to correct the situation, when we proceed to throw the entire preferences into the discard? It seems to me that we are setting out to have a permanent and ever-increasing problem with our American trade if we throw away all the advantages we now possess through the British preferences in the sterling area. We must put forth a greater effort to save the British commonwealth market, which directly provides jobs for a million Canadians. We will want the government to explain clearly just how these agreements are going to resolve the present crisis with -which we are dealing.
As the leader of the Progressive Conservative party, I suggest that we ought to be considering other positive measures. Among other things, I suggest the following as the program that we ought to follow.
First, we should explore the possibility of preserving more of our greatest markets than the government's present policies are likely to preserve. Our essential market for farm and primary products has been and is in the sterling area. Are the government's present plans predicated on British bankruptcy? It looks to me as if they are. I think without a British market, our economy will suffer a severe deflationary process and our standards of living will be greatly impaired.
Second, we should relieve our present shortages and the ever-mounting inflationary pressures by getting production going in Canada with the same determination and energy which we showed in the war.
Third, we should try to arrange with the United Kingdom for the production on a priority basis of those supplies from which we now are cut off through no fault of the Canadian people.
Fourth, we should accept the opportunity offered in article XXIY of the Geneva agreement to try to protect our great stake in the sterling area by exploring the possibilities of an acceptable customs union with the other British nations or some modified form thereof on a basis which will secure both our own individual interests and the interests of the group as a whole. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I am placing emphasis upon the great market which we have had all these years, in connection with which we have always had favourable balances of trade, a market which we are losing through the government's exchange of letters. I think we ought to try to save as much of that market as we can.
Tariffs and Trade

Fifth, we should attempt to get a greater return in jobs and in profits out of our natural resources by adopting the following measures:
(a)	By requiring a higher degree of processing of our primary products before export from Canada;
(b)	By dispersing our industry throughout the nation in order to achieve a better balanced and more stable economy.;
(c)	By making in Canada those things which we are well able to make, but which we hitherto have bought abroad;
(d)	By in these ways creating the basis for a substantial enlargement of our population which will, in turn, make a stronger and wealthier Canada.
(e)	We should embark upon a great enterprise of scientific research and development for the greater and more efficient utilization of the resources with which this nation is endowed and to enable us to keep at home those fine young Canadians who now go abroad to enrich other countries. Let us use Canada's brains in Canada, for Canada.
I had thought of proposing an amendment to this resolution, not in any controversial waj', but simply to indicate that we feel that the action which is being taken as a result of the government's exchange of letters is likely to lose more of the British market than we should. However, I shall not do that. But I do want to place the amendment on the record as our attitude toward the resolution before us.
As justification for the procedure which I have mentioned, I should like to quote a paragraph from a great Liberal-I use the word in the broadest possible sense-free trade journal, The Economist. Under date of November 27, 1947, the following paragraph appeared under the heading, "Trade under the new tariff":
To assess the exact consequences for the future of world trade of a tariff agreement between 23 nations, which has involved 106 sets of bilateral negotiations between the parties over a period of six months, and is now set down in an agreement containing 34 articles and two volumes of schedules weighing eight pounds, is an impossible task. The agreement arrives at the very time that Britain is adopting bilateral trading practices as a matter of self-defence-
In self-defence Great Britain has been resorting to bilateral trade practices. We are washing out that procedure here. I am not attempting at the moment to say whether Great Britain was right or wrong or whether we are right or wrong. The article goes on:
-but despite this and all the other impediments to the free flow of international commerce, multilateral trade relationships still extend over a

large part of the -world and account for a significant share of world commerce. The extreme complexity of these relationships means that the balance of gain and sacrifice cannot be worked out by any process of simple arithmetic; formal figuring alone would require the mathematician's apparatus of simultaneous equations, but calculations of this sort will be far less important, in the end, than the effects of the agreement as a whole upon the quantum of World trade. World trade could increase and leave some countries poorer, but that is hardly a consequence which is likely to apply to Britain.
I read that extract because it comes from a journal which is respected by many people.
I now repeat what I said earlier, that, after the British agreement is separated from the Geneva agreements, it is evident that the government is proceeding in a wrong manner when they ask us to deal with the Geneva matter under two resolutions. Proceeding in the way they are it can only mean that we shall be denied an opportunity to study in committee the general provisions of the agreement as outlined in the first resolution.
I close with one question. What then are the alternatives before the nation? The government has put forward a program which many think can end only in the further impoverishment of the nation. There surely is an alternative to that. Whether these agreements are approved or not-and I hope we find we can approve them-I suggest that we should have a more expanding program. I suggest that it is to be found in a more positive expansion program for the maximum development of Canada's wealth and resources for the benefit of Canada.
