speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since we knew that we were going to discuss the Geneva agreements today, I have asked myself why we are discussing treaties 'that do not become fully effective at the present time when we have so many other important problems before us. I feel that we should be dealing with problems that immediately affect the people of Canada rather than these treaties which we do not have to make fully effective immediately. It seems to me that the pressing problems affecting our country require the immediate attention of this house and they should have been placed first upon the agenda or order paper for this session.
No matter how beneficial these agreements may appear to be on the surface-and there are some good things in the Geneva treaties- they simply cannot become fully effective until Europe has been rehabilitated, until the nations of Europe are in a position to trade with the other countries that have entered into these Geneva agreements. Until that condition comes about, these agreements do not mean a

Tariffs and Trade
great deal, either to Canada or to the other countries which have signed them provisionally. So I say that, in spite of any good thing which may be found in this agreement, its success depends entirely upon world recovery.
This evening the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), if I may say so, introduced one of those old-fashioned tariff debates that we had about ten years ago. You know, Mr. Speaker, when I used to listen to the tariff debates in this house ten years ago or read them in Hansard before, that my reaction was this, that, in spite of all the talk about tariffs, my hon. friends to the right, at that time the Conservative party believed in high tariffs and said so, while our friends of the Liberal party always maintained a tariff that was high. I found it very difficult indeed to find any distinction or any differences between the two parties, when in power, in that particular field.
I agree with all that has been said today in regard to the necessity of economic co-operation among all the nations of the world. I also agree that multilateral trade is a very desirable objective that we should do all we can to aid and further, but may I point out that at the moment there is no possibility of multilateral trade on a world basis; that all we can hope for at the moment, apart from trade treaties altogether, is that the sickness of the world may be cured and that we may be able to trade more fully with one another to the advantage of us all.
Multilateral trade, then, cannot be promoted immediately by this agreement. Indeed, many of the nations that have entered into the agreement are themselves as nations buying under national import and export boards the goods they need to meet the needs of their peoples, and we ourselves in Canada are entering into agreements as a nation for the supplying of food and so forth on a long-term basis. I am of the opinion that, in spite of all the fine things that are said about the Geneva treaty, export and import boards will be used by nations more and more as time goes on. in spite of anything one may think regarding some provisions of these particular agreements.
I agree that Canada's historic trading was done on what was known as the Atlantic triangle. We sold goods in vast quantities to Great Britain, our best customer, and bought in vast quantities from the United States, and as long as Great Britain occupied the position she did in world affairs we were able to continue that type of trading. But Great Britain has now sold many of her overseas assets which brought her the goods of the world in payment of interest on her investments abroad. Because of war necessity-our necessity as well
as hers-she has disposed of many of her overseas assets, and she is not now receiving the amount she once received as the carrying nation of the world in the realm of shipping. Her great financial institutions and insurance companies are no longer in the all-powerful position they once occupied. Therefore we find ourselves in a different position too.
But most of all, Mr. Speaker, I believe this, that the future of Canada's trade and the future welfare of the world depend upon the willingness of the United States to accept the new role that the world has assigned to her as the result of two great wars, and in tying ourselves to the United States economy as we are doing under this treaty we must beware lest the United States does not fulfil that role.
I looked at the trade balance for last year, 1946, and what did I find? I found that last year the United States exported some $21 billion worth of goods and received in return from the rest of the world only some $8 billion worth of goods, leaving the world in debt to the United States in terms of money to the amount of some $13 billion. Even under this Geneva treaty the United States tariff will still be relatively high, and the world will find it very difficult for many goods to climb over the high tariff wall erected around that great country.
Tonight, for example, we heard of the excise tax imposed by Canada. It does not come under this agreement, but we are told that the excise tax is to be added to the cost of Canadian goods entering the United States, That is a twenty-five per cent excise tax, or a proportion of that tax will be chargeable in the form of duty against Canadian goods entering the United States. So it is really a new tariff wall erected against certain Canadian goods which we have been making during the war, electrical supplies and so on, which we have been exporting to the United States. To. my mind, that is an indication that this treaty-may be a broken reed upon which the government is inclined to lean and upon which we-are building so much hope for the future.
I doubt very much whether many members, of the house have been able to do more than I have done with regard to these treaties. I have simply been able to give them a cursory reading, skim through them instead of' scanning them, and I say to the Prime Minister and to the government that, before-this house is asked to approve the resolution approving the Geneva agreements, in, which I am willing to admit, as I have already said, there are, I believe, good things, the house should have the opportunity of finding; out exactly what this treaty involves in every particular. In other words, I think a decision.
Tariffs and Trade

on this resolution and on the treaty should be delayed until parliament reconvenes and then the whole matter should be referred to a special committee of the house or to the committee that has been set up for such a purpose, the banking and commerce committee of this house. There hon. members would be able to call the gentlemen who represented Canada at Geneva, the men who actually negotiated this treaty, the men who know what every line of the treaty actually means so far as Canada and the rest of the world are concerned. I think that none of us should be prepared to give his adherence to a treaty of this description individually or collectively on behalf of Canada until we understand the implication of every line of the treaty.
As I have said, I have been able to give the treaty only a cursory reading, to skim the surface of it, but even so I note that there are a good many escape clauses in the treaty itself, put there presumably in the interests of various countries. As I said this afternoon, one of these escape clauses we might have used to our advantage until at least January 1, 1949, for the general agreement states, in article XIV, section 6 (a), that the provisions of the agreement relating to nondiscrimination shall not come into force "in respect of import restrictions applied by any contracting party ... in order to safeguard its external financial position and balance of payments" until January 1, 1949; "provided that this period may, with the concurrence of the contracting parties, be extended for such further periods as they may specify in respect of any contracting party whose supply of convertible currency is inadequate." That is the very position in which Canada is today.
We were told that Washington put pressure .ipon Canada to put the excise tax into effect. We were told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) this afternoon, but not in those terms, that the United States government laid so much stress upon the non-discriminatory clause of this treaty that it was advisable for Canada to put it into effect. In other words, we are in danger of falling more and more under the domination of the United States. I have the greatest respect for the American people. We have lived on friendly relations with them for well over a century, and whenever one visits the United States one gets a kindly and hospitable welcome. But no one more than the Prime Minister has adopted policies designed to deliver us from the domination of Downing street, and I do not want to exchange the domination of Washington for the domination of Downing street. Let us not

escape from one to be dominated by the other. But we have had two indications today of pressure brought upon this country by the United States.
The United States has a new role to fulfil in the world. I wonder if she will fulfil it. I remember the pledge given to the American people by the President of the United States some months ago. I listened to him on the radio one evening some months ago, and he said that before there were any substantial tariff reductions in the United States, the interests involved would be given an opportunity to appear before the appropriate committee of the senate to make their representations. He assured the American people

as I say, I heard him over the radio-that he would not approve reductions until the interests affected had been heard by a senate committee.
We do not follow that method in Canada, and I am not asking that all interests involved shall appear before a committee of this house or of the senate of Canada. What I am asking tonight is that, before this house is asked to approve this treaty, in any particular and under any resolution, the matter be referred either to a special committee of this house or to the banking and commerce committee for a thorough investigation.
Let us bear this in mind when discussing trade treaties and particularly a treaty with the United States, that to a very large extent our economy is competitive with that of the United States. Our fruit growers, wheat growers and dairy producers are competitive with similar producers in the United States, and I think that, before we tie ourselves up to any particular treaty which involves us in the American economy, we should be sure that we have something of a long-term agreement. The year 1952 is not far away, and when I view the lobbying that goes on at Washington -thank goodness we do not get that kind here-

speechtext: We get some.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
We get a little but not the same kind as at Washington, where all kinds of organizations keep permanent lobbyists around congress. The powerful farm block of the middle west, for example, will not view with equanimity, even if they do at first, in the interest of world trade, competition by our western wheat and western farm produce with the commodities which they produce in the middle west. The same applies to fishermen and to other interests in the United States, including, as my hon. friend suggests, the fruit growers of that country.
There is one other thing I wish to bring to the attention of the house. Not in relation

Tariffs and Trade
to this treaty particularly, but generally under any form of economic arrangements in the world as organized today, I am fearful of the influence of cartels. International cartels are organized by national private monopolies. We know perfectly well that many of the articles which we can produce in Canada are controlled by international cartels, and Canadians are actually prevented from exporting certain articles that are controlled by international cartels. I am not asking the hon. gentleman to take my word for that. Our own commissioner, appointed under the Combines Investigation Act, submitted an excellent factual report to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) some time ago. A reading of that report-1 hope all hon. gentlemen have read it-indicates clearljr that that some Canadian industries have been prohibited from exporting to countries abroad, certain types of material made in Canada, quite a long list of them, in the chemical industry, for example. Cartels know no law. Monopolies and cartels can entirely neutralize any advantages that we might get under trade treaties.
I do not want to prolong the discussion tonight because, frankly, as I say, I have merely skimmed this treaty. We have been given it only since the house met. Of course, I have read some of the press releases, some of the news items, and as well as I was able I followed the newspaper reports of the discussions at Geneva, where I know that we were very well represented. One realizes that the Canadian officials under Mr. Wilgress, who represented us there, were representing Canada well. I have confidence in them. But they have not to take the responsibility for the treaty; we have to take it. If it is good, we shall get credit for it, they will not; if it is bad, we shall get the blame for it, they will not.
What I really rose to say was this. As far as we in this party are concerned, the party for which I speak, we want a thorough inquiry into all the implications of the treaty; and once more I repeat what I have already said, that, before we are asked to cast a single vote in approval or disapproval of this particular treaty, we should have a thorough investigation. Let us have it where we can call the men who agreed to and, to some extent, wrote the provisions of this treaty. Let us call them before a committee of the bouse where we can go into the matter with great thoroughness. Then we shall feel, whether we approve or disapprove this treaty,
that we have done our best for the people who have sent us to this chamber to do the best we can for Canada and the world.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is not often I hear a speech delivered in tne House of Commons which I feel I should be glad to have delivered myself, but I think we have had one exception to that rule in the speech which has been delivered by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Coldwell). I think he has admirably expressed the whole case and I should like to commend him for what he has said. I wish there could have been as much realistic thinking all through the house two years ago when we were struggling over the Bretton Woods agreement as there appears to be at the present time. We should have avoided an exceedingly dangerous and costly experiment, I would say an exceedingly dangerous blunder, in accepting what I consider to be a pernicious agreement. I believe the members of the house will discover that before we have finished.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext: We have discovered it already.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Yes. I believe a good many have discovered it already. I think we can lay this down as a sound fundamental principle to be applied throughout the world: Trade must be not only free but also safe. I have heard nothing said tonight, I have heard nothing said in this house, regarding the matter of making trade safe. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said nothing about that. If the nations of the world are to be truly free from fear they must have the ability to trade and be safe while they trade. Any nation must be not only free to trade but also free from fear in exercising its freedom to trade.
There are a good many today who are wondering why the bitterness, the hatred and extreme feeling all over the world. I will dare wager that the cause lies right in the fact that nothing has been done to establish the principle which I have just laid down. The nations are mortally afraid of the danger in trade.
May I refer to the figures which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) gave regarding the foreign trade of the United States? The United States annually sells about $12 billion more goods than she buys. Hon. members can weigh that fact with the most earnest consideration and see what they conceive to be the logical conclusion from that dangerous fact. Because the United States annually sells $12 billion more goods than she buys, the rest of the world every year goes 812 billion into an adverse trade
Tariffs and Trade

balance with the United States. Somebody incurs that adverse trade balance. We ourselves have incurred upwards of a billion of it this year. The realization that such a possibility is always a danger constitutes a haunting fear to all the nations, from Canada to Russia. The nations, in sheer self-defence, have had to resort to tariffs, quotas, exchange controls and manipulations of currencies or downright embargoes; otherwise their economies would have been destroyed.
The astonishing thing, observable in the discussions leading up to these so-called peace measures, such as Bretton Woods and the united nations charter, is that so many like Morgenthau and Roosevelt have contended that when nations put up trade barriers and use exchange control and other means to defend their economies these nations are engaging in industrial or economic aggression. That is one of the most amazing lies ever perpetrated upon the earth. When nations to ensure economic self-defence against a powerful nation such as the United States put up trade barriers to protect themselves are accused tf economic aggression it is simply appalling thing, Mr. Speaker. And to think that we should live in an age in which that sort of thing can be done and in which so many can be deluded by it!
May I just say a word in explanation of this remarkable situation? About 1922 the United States administration began to place a special interpretation upon the expression, "the most-favoured-nation clause". Britain had for generations used what was called "the most-favoured-nation clause". As Britain interpreted the clause, it simply meant that if any nation were willing to grant concessions to British goods entering that nation's economy, then Britain would grant a similar concession to that nation's goods entering Britain's economy; consequently the mostfavoured-nation clause or the most-favourednation treatment meant granting a special privilege or favour to that nation.
About 1922, I repeat, the United States began to put a different interpretation upon the expression entirely. They began to say that if any nation lowered its tariff or granted any concession to any other nation, then that nation was in duty bound to grant the same concession to every other nation. This was an interpretation of the most-favoured-nation clause which was fraught with the gravest danger. The United States administration has maintained that interpretation right down to the present time.
Under the United States interpretation of the most-favoured-nation clause, it was a matter of forcing the nation granting a con-

cession to another nation, to grant the same concession to the United States or to any other nation that might demand it. As a means of popularizing the most-favourednation clause as the United States interpreted it, the United States began to use the expression "non-discrimination" to describe it. They said that if a nation granted a special concession-we will say that Brazil granted a special concession to Great Britain and that Great Britain in return granted a similar concession to Brazil, then, if Brazil and Britain did not grant the same concession to the United States, Brazil and Britain were accused of "discriminating" against the United States. Thus the United States administration began to work for the application of what they called "the principle of non-discrimination."
But that is not all. Roosevelt, on the Atlantic in 1941, when he met with war-worn Churchill to draft the Atlantic charter, directed his efforts toward constraining Churchill into accepting the destruction of empire preferences because, as Roosevelt said, empire preferences were discrimination against the United States. Churchill resisted successfully, much to his honour.
Then the United States administration caused the Bretton Woods agreement and the Dumbarton Oaks agreement to be drafted as two instruments through which to obtain the "non-discrimination" objective which they endeavoured to attain through Churchill.
The Bretton Woods agreement is based upon non-discrimination, or the application of the United States interpretation of the mostfavoured-nation clause. The Bretton Woods agreement was aimed at breaking down the power of the accepting nations to use the defences against adverse trade balances which they had long used, such as tariffs, quotas, exchange restrictions and so forth. But in the Bretton Woods agreement there was not one single thing to protect the nations from adverse trade balances and their evil effects. I pointed this out, Mr. Speaker, in March and April of 1945 when we were contemplating the San Francisco conference. I pointed out the causes of war, namely, adverse trade balances and the danger thereof. I pointed out that in the Bretton Woods agreement and in the Dumbarton Oaks agreement there was no provision whatsoever for safeguarding the weaker nations against the encroachments of the strong in the matter of trade.
Then the United States high-pressured the nations into accepting the united nations charter. This charter was supposed to be the means of obtaining peace in the world. As a matter of fact, it was nothing but a United

Tarifts and Trade
States commercial instrument to force upon the nations that accepted it the principle of non-discrimination in trade, which meant the application of the United States interpretation of the most-favoured-nation clause. You will find that indicated in the purposes of the united nations charter. Primarily, as I have said, the object of the united nations charter was simply to take away the power of nations to defend themselves against United States industrial aggression. Non-discrimination is only a weasel expression, meaning the application of the most-favoured-nation clause according to the United States interpretation of 1922.
Since then, there have been several trade conferences. There was one in the fall of 1946, to which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred. There was one in Geneva from April 10 to October 30 of this year, if I recall correctly, and there is one now convened at Havana. Each of these trade conferences was aimed to add threads to the spider web of intrigue wrapped around Britain and the members of the British commonwealth, and other nations that happened to be involved, to render them helpless to protect their economies from the incursion of United States goods. The object pursued by the United States throughout all these negotiations. insistently and relentlessly, implacably and callously, has been to force the whole world into a condition of utter helplessness before United States industrial aggression and penetration.
These may seem to be very strong words, Mr. Speaker, but I urge hon. members to give the most careful consideration to each of these measures to see whether or not they do not find justification for what I have said. I believe without question that they will find such evidence. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), in what I thought was a strong speech tonight, showed quite clearly that he suspected the existence of danger in these treaties.
Still greater anxiety was injected into the world situation by a statement made by President Roosevelt in a radio broadcast in October, 1944, when he said something to this effect: "I intend to find jobs for sixty million Americans by tripling our exports." Well, Mr. Speaker, if the United States was already exporting so abundantly to the world and President Roosevelt proposed to increase those exports three times, will someone tell me where would be the markets for any of the other nations?
What is to happen to nations with weaker economies? How are those nations to avoid
disastrous trade balances? How repay the debts into which they must fall as a result? By the time Canada, for example, finishes repaying the adverse trade balance we have incurred this year we shall have gained a great deal of experience. I wonder if anyone can see how in the world this country can repay that adverse trade balance of S900 million. I should be happy to hear a suggestion from anyone who thinks he has found how we can do it. Meanwhile, how in the world, then, are the nations to obtain the United States dollars they need?
What happens to a nation when it falls into an adverse trade balance? As the leader of the official opposition pointed out, we have had an adverse trade balance almost always since 1867 in Canada. Well, ultimately that adverse trade balance will result in something like this: The United States in effect will say to Canada, after we have endeavoured without success for five or six years to pay off the $900 million, "You will never be able to pay off this adverse trade balance, Canada; so just give us Canadian dollars and we will invest those dollars in Canadian securities of various kinds; your gold mines, your coal mines, your forests, your railroads and anything else you happen to have in the way of fixed assets of value." Thereby what are called United States "investments" in Canada will increase. If this process goes on indefinitely the interest payments we shall have to make on those investments every year will become greater and greater until the millstone around our necks becomes impossible for us to maintain and we go under. Then we utterly lose our economic freedom, and ultimately lose our political freedom. In the light of a situation like this, how can nations such as France. Czechoslovakia, or any other of the ordinary nations maintain their economic freedom? How can they maintain their political freedom? How can they maintain prosperity?
For the United States I am going to say this, because probably certain officials of that country will read these remarks. To American people I say: "I was born in the United States and I love your country. I am interested in its welfare. I also love Canada. I say the people of the United States will have to think very seriously of what they will do after they destroy the economies of the other nations of the world. Where will they find the markets they now feel they need? What will be the ultimate effect on the United States herself? Will they not have another depression there from which they will find it utterly impossible to extricate themselves? And is it not time now, before widespread disaster strikes, to take thought and do something about this matter, something different from what the United States is now endeavouring to do?"
Tariffs and Trade

What will probably happen is this:	If we
should go down into another depression we shall have communism in every country. This will result in a world communist state. Then what will be the result? A dictatorship by a certain group of gentlemen who will gain access to the reins of power. The freedom of the world will be gone. This is more serious than I like to think about.
Why is it the United States constitutes such a danger to the various nations of the world? There are several reasons which every hon. member will immediately bring to mind. First, there is the size of the territory of the United States. Next, there is the richness, the variety of resources which makes the United States almost self-sufficient so that it does not need the goods which would have to be sent to that country to pay for the adverse balances which other nations incurred. Then, there are upwards of 145,000,000 people of the United States, giving her producers a market which enables them to sell enough goods within their own nation to coveT their overhead and make a profit so that they can almost dump the remainder of their goods anywhere in the world. Then, there, is the industrialization of the United States, which was greatly augmented during the war. Vast factories were built to produce tremendous quantities of goods which were necessary during the war, but which perhaps will not find such a ready market now that the war is over. Finally, there is the financial power of the United States, the accumulation of finance and their skill and ability in financing production.
The question will be asked:	What could
be done? I do not wish to go into details in that regard, but let me give some figures which may help hon. members to think this matter through, as they helped me. In 1918 the United States produced $60,000 million worth of goods. During that same year all the money distributed in the United States in wages, salaries, dividends and by every other means amounted to S45.000 million. Of that 845,000 million about $5,000 million went into life insurance or in other ways became more or less passive as far as purchasing goods was concerned. This left $20,000 million worth of goods in the United States with no money to buy them. What was to become of the $20,000 million worth of goods? The United States still faces that kind of problem, only in a highly aggravated form. What is she going to do? Well, I would say the only wise thing the United States can possibly do is develop a means of distributing purchasing power within her own country, to enable her own people to use her goods as far as they fMr. Blackmore.]
wish. Surely if she can lend money to France, let us say, and that money is good for the purchase of United States goods, the same money distributed among the people of the United States would be equally good for the purchase of United States products.
With respect to the things which the United States would still have to export or may wish to export, may I offer this suggestion? If the United States were to take, for instance, the adverse trade balance incurred in Canada this year, amounting to S900 million, and were to say, "Canada, you do not need to worry about that $900 million which you have incurred as an adverse trade balance; we will just keep it on our records as a credit. We will not charge you interest on it. We will not embarrass you in any way. Some of these days probably you will have lumber or pulp wood or something else that we will want, and then we will accept it in payment of this debt. And if we do not take the goods in payment of this $900 million debt after seven years have expired, we will cancel the $900 million debt-we will just wash it out" -I say that if the United States would take that attitude and a similar attitude in its dealings with every nation of the world, she would have established what might be called contra-credits in each of those nations with which she might trade. And if every nation in the world, including Canada, did the same sort of thing, it would become possible to visualize a state of affairs in which the trading of the world would be beneficial to every nation.
Some will say, "How can a nation do things like that? How can it give goods away?" A vast quantity of goods which the United States is already selling abroad will never be paid for, for the simple reason that the United States will never want goods in payment for them. Indeed, she will put up tariff barriers to keep out those goods, because they would compete with her own goods. What happened in connection with the debt Great Britain owed to the United States as a result of the first world war? That debt never was repaid, not because Great Britain did not want to repay it; rather it was because the United States refused to accept goods in payment.
The British have sold goods on credit to the extent of billions upon billions of pounds, and have never received anything back. They have cancelled those debts. So the proposal is thoroughly logical; it is something that has been tried. Now if something like contra-credits were provided for in these trade treaties we are now considering we would see a way out of the difficulties which at present are rendering conditions impossible for the weaker

Tariffs and Trade
economies in the world. We would have something worthy of the attention, of this House of Commons, something that would have a chance of evading and preventing war.
But the measures we are considering now will never prevent war; they will cause war. Everyone must realize that Canada is in a far more dangerous position today than, she would be if she were not tied up to the Bretton Woods agreement. And she will be in a far more dangerous position if she becomes committed to these Geneva treaties, and especially the general treaties; because there are in them clauses which bind Canada still further, in the same way as the Bretton Woods agreement bound her. So I would suggest that if the nations would establish a system of multilateral contra-credits to take care of the adverse trade balances which develop as a result of trade, then I would feel some hope for the future of the world.
In closing, I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in his request that the study of these treaties be submitted to a committee and given the most careful scrutiny-something far, far better than we had when we were considering the Bretton Woods agreement. I think to my dying day I shall look back with disgust and shame upon the farcical performance when we considered the Bretton Woods agreement in the banking and commerce committee. There was not a ghost of a chance given for reasonable and fair consideration of the meaning and implication of the various sections of that act. It was rushed through in a very short time. All hon. members need to do is to get from the library the Final Act of Bretton Woods, and proceed to read it through. Let them see how long it takes to read it. Then I would suggest they read it again, until they have some idea of its meaning, and some idea of how long it would take a man to understand that Bretton Woods agreement. Then I would ask them to recall how it was jammed through the House of Commons in about five days.

speechtext:
I hope we shall have a real study' of this present measure, and not under such high pressure that it will be a disgrace to the House of Commons. If, as was hinted by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the United States is putting pressure upon our nation to oblige us to accept measures of this sort, then the sooner we know about it the better. And let the matter be known throughout the world in its bare, simple nakedness; because if we have to go down to
destruction, then let us at least know where we are going, and why. Let us see if we have at least the courage and the stamina which has characterized our fathers back through the centuries. Surely we have not fought two wars in order to be enslaved by a series of base measures like Bretton Woods-surely notl Just as an indication of how difficult it is to make an adequate study of these treaties, let me say that I took the trouble to count through the number of pages involved. Each hon. member upon returning to this session received a set of five books with a total of 1,431 pages of closely typewritten material. This is the third day of our session. And we are supposed to have been able to read this material through and to have formed some sort of estimate of the implications in those many pages in this brief space of time! On the face of it, we have an indication that all is not fair and square.
Why all this secrecy? Why all this haste? Once more I suggest most earnestly that every possible facility be given for the most careful study. I suggest, further, that hon. members be ready to refuse sternly those treaties until such modifications are made in them as will render them safe for the world and fit to' be accepted by men whose sons died on many a battlefield overseas; whose sons died for freedom and not for slavery, such as these agreements involve; whose sons died for peace, not for war such as these measures if accepted render inevitable.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE AT GENEVA, 1947- APPROVAL OF GENERAL AGREEMENT

Mr. Speaker, I have followed with a good deal of interest the debate as carried on by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and by the leaders of other groups, and I have been impressed particularly by the lack of appreciation of the importance of this agreement.
Here we have the most far-reaching lowering of trade barriers ever accomplished in the history of international trade. We are blamed by opposition groups for having called parliament together to consider this agreement.
I remind hon. members that the agreement has already been executed by eighteen countries and comes into effect on January 1 of next year. I wonder what parliament would have said if we had not brought hon. members together to discuss the terms of the agreement before it became effective. Apparently the impression is abroad that the government is attempting to force the agreement through parliament without adequate discussion and without consideration by a committee. There was nothing in the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to indicate anything of the sort. He has asked me to say
Tariffs and Trade

that the government will invite the fullest discussion of this resolution and the resolution which follows it and of the bill which follows the two resolutions, in committee, at any stage the house may wish.
As a matter of fact, two or three days ago the Prime Minister and the leader of the government in the senate decided that the other chamber would proceed at once to set up a committee to study the trade agreements. I rather think that committee has already been established, and will commence its work at once. As I understood it from the leader of the government in the senate, the plan is that that committee will bring before it government experts who will explain every phase of the agreements, and be' subjected to any questioning that hon. members of the senate may wish to place before them.

speechtext:
My hon. friend would not understand this. He said that he did not, and I agree with him. We have had alternative measures presented. I think the one that will perhaps Startle the businessmen of this country more than anything else is the alternative offered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) of a customs union within the British empire. There may have been times when it would have been proper to discuss that alternative, but it seems to me that that time is hardly the present when all the nations of the British empire except South Africa have been obliged to restrict buying and to adopt severe austerity programs.
Obviously I cannot finish my remarks this evening and I think, in order to do justice to the subject, I should have an uninterrupted forty minutes in which to place the principles of the agreements before the house. Therefore, I would ask the indulgence of the house to permit me to adjourn tlhe debate at this time.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
